items.body: Jesu Aparicio is a Spanish artist who sees himself first and foremost as a DJ, and only secondly as a producer. He has been active in the Spanish club scene for years and won me over this year with his album “Human Control”. The album was released on Jesu’s own label, Espacio Cielo, in collaboration with Mots Music. The name Parissior may not ring a bell for many, but I highly recommend this work to anyone with an interest in Dark-Techno and EBM. The album’s title and theme reflect the increasingly complex relationship between humans, technology, control, and the systems that shape our daily lives. By combining dark electronic sounds with an atmosphere that is both unsettling and intriguing, Parissior creates music that invites the listener to look beyond the surface. The album evokes the atmosphere and danceability of the 1990s Frankfurt Techno scene while adding a distinctly contemporary twist. For me, this record is one of this year’s best discoveries, making it the perfect time to meet the artist behind Parissior and talk to him about “Human Control”, his influences, and his approach to music. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Parissior interview Q: Could you give us some background on your musical activities, which apparently began quite some time ago as a DJ and eventually evolved into producing, leading to the Parissior project? Jesu: I began DJing professionally in my native Cantabria in 2001, playing Techno and House under my own name, ‘Jesu Aparicio’. In 2004, I moved to Salamanca, where I became a resident DJ at several venues, including Cubic Club, Submarino and Beatz. Those years were a major learning experience for me and gave me a much deeper understanding of the music industry. I eventually opened my own venue, Clavel Ocho, which featured an upstairs floor dedicated to Electronic music called Espacio Cielo – the name I would later revive for my record label. I started producing around 2004 and, over the years, explored many different styles and released music under several aliases. Altogether, I have released more than 600 tracks. I have always considered myself a DJ first and a producer second, although these days I actually spend more time producing music than performing as a DJ. Around 2011, I began to feel restricted by playing the same styles, so I created the Parissior alias as a way to broaden my musical horizons. It allowed me to explore funkier and more cosmic sounds, as well as Electro and Italo-Disco, eventually moving towards the EBM-influenced sound that has become an important part of the project’s identity. Q: Personally, I find it interesting that you moved into music production after starting out as a DJ – a role that naturally exposes you to a vast amount of music. This perhaps also helps explain the eclectic nature of your own work. What did your experience as a DJ bring to your approach to music-making, and what were some of your key influences and muses? Jesu: As a DJ, I have always been very eclectic and curious, and I have always enjoyed collecting music from a wide range of genres: ’80s music, Funk and Soul, Disco, Electro, House, Techno, Big Beat, Breaks… Salamanca had many clubs and bars, each with a very distinct musical identity, so playing there pushed you to dig deeper, discover new sounds and adapt to very different audiences. Being exposed to such a vast amount of music has undoubtedly had a major influence on the way I produce. You learn to recognize the formulas and ideas that make each genre work, and then reinterpret and adapt them to your own musical language. My influences have naturally evolved over the years, but I could never leave out Joy Division and New Order, Talking Heads, The Prodigy, The Chemical Brothers, Pet Shop Boys, Andrew Weatherall, Primal Scream or LCD Soundsystem, among many others. Q: You released the album “Human Control” this year, which, as I understand it, was not originally conceived as an album. How did it all come about, and how did the concept of “Human Control” take shape? Or did the concept emerge only afterwards, almost imposing itself on the music? Jesu: As you rightly say, the album was not initially planned as such. I had three tracks that I had deliberately held back from releasing on any label because they felt more personal, less focused on the dancefloor, and did not really fit with any of the EPs I had previously released. Almost without realizing it, I had incorporated phrases and messages into those tracks that shared a certain underlying theme: a defense of the analogue world and a critique of the artificiality and falsehood that often surround today’s digital culture and social media. Once I recognized that common thread, I decided to compose a series of new tracks around those original three and gradually shape the whole thing into an album. The first track I created with that intention was “Human Control.” It features a sample from a speech by Greta Thunberg at the UN Climate Action Summit, in which she delivers a passionate and somewhat dramatic rebuke to the world’s leaders. That track ultimately gave both the album and its central concept a clear identity. Q: What can you tell us about the writing and production process behind the album? What did you focus on most, and what were the different stages you went through to bring “Human Control” to completion? What tools and equipment did you work with, and what were the biggest challenges along the way? Jesu: One of the album’s defining features – and also its biggest challenge – was the decision to deliberately limit the amount of hardware and software I used on each track. I find that working within those kinds of restrictions forces me to be more creative, especially compared with having thousands of possibilities available in the form of plug-ins. My process was generally to choose a small palette of sound sources for each track, record the main parts, and then reshape and develop them through processing. For example, every synthesizer part on “True Connection” came from the Waldorf Pulse 2. Most of the basslines on the album were created with an analogue clone of the Roland SH-101, which I also used to design many of the drum sounds, while the Acid lines came from the Behringer TD-3. Another synthesizer that played a major role throughout the album was the Model D, and I also incorporated parts I had recorded years earlier with my Roland JX-3P. On the software side, I used Ableton’s stock plug-ins alongside Massive and Omnisphere. Massive was the only synthesizer used on “Human Control,” while Omnisphere appears more sparingly on some of the other tracks, mainly providing polyphonic textures. I also enjoy running synthesizers through effects pedals to create new tones and textures, while the vocals were processed using the Roland VT-4 and a variety of VST effects. Ultimately, the main focus was to get as much character and variety as possible from a relatively small and carefully chosen set of tools. Q: With this album, you explore themes such as digital identity, technology, artificial validation, and the relationship between humans and machines. Could you tell us a little more about these themes, and to what extent did they influence your decision to release the album on vinyl? To me, the physical format almost feels like a response to – or a reaction against – the increasingly digital nature of our lives. And if so, why vinyl rather than cassette? Jesu: That was exactly the idea. Releasing the album on vinyl was, in many ways, a reaction against the digitalisation of almost every aspect of our lives. Particularly since the pandemic, it often feels as though people’s lives have been reduced to the online alter egos they create on platforms such as Instagram – showing the world only what they want others to see and projecting lifestyles that they are not necessarily living in reality. Releasing a record on vinyl had also been unfinished business for me with Espacio Cielo, so my own album felt like the perfect opportunity to take that step. There was an economic reason as well: digital sales are falling every year as listening increasingly shifts towards streaming platforms such as Spotify, yet the royalties these services pay are extremely unfair. Sometimes you barely earn enough to buy a hamburger, which makes it very difficult for an independent label to remain financially sustainable. I also feel that digital music is more ephemeral. It disappears more quickly, becomes outdated faster and struggles to hold people’s attention. A vinyl record has a physical presence and a sense of permanence: people tend to spend more time with it, and it can remain part of their lives for years. In that sense, the format became a natural extension of the album’s concept. To be honest, I never seriously considered releasing it on cassette. It is a very nostalgic format, but I also think that very few people still own the equipment needed to play tapes. Of course, the same issue exists to some extent with vinyl, but many DJs have kept their Technics turntables, and the fact that the company has released new models such as the MK7 gives me some reason for optimism. Vinyl also has a much stronger connection to my own history as a DJ and to the culture surrounding this music. From now on, we plan to slow down the label’s digital release schedule and gradually release more records on vinyl. Who knows – perhaps in a few years we will release exclusively on vinyl. It is something I am seriously considering. Q: Where do you draw the line today between human control and the control we voluntarily surrender to technology? In what sense do you see the title and concept of “Human Control” as a warning, an observation, or perhaps even a personal confession? How do you see humans evolving alongside technological progress, and what role do you think the musician will play in that relationship? Jesu: That boundary is becoming increasingly blurred. There is no denying that we will benefit enormously from technological progress and that it will make many aspects of our lives easier. However, when it comes to art and culture, I believe we need to preserve certain principles and ensure that convenience and automation do not replace human intention, creativity and genuine expression. In that sense, “Human Control” is both an observation and a warning. Technology itself is not the enemy; the real question is how much control and creative autonomy we are willing to surrender to it. We should remain the ones making the decisions, with technology serving as a tool rather than dictating the creative process. At the same time, I think a counter-movement is beginning to emerge – one that will bring back a greater appreciation for craftsmanship, physical formats and live music. I am already seeing clubs programming exclusively live sets, as well as all-vinyl nights, which I find very encouraging. Perhaps the musician’s role in this new relationship will be precisely to preserve that human element: spontaneity, imperfection and a genuine connection with the audience. Q: Do you also perform your Parissior tracks live, or do they mainly form part of your DJ sets? How does that work in practice, and what can we expect from Parissior in the near future? Jesu: I have always considered myself more of a DJ than a producer, even though, since the pandemic, I have actually spent more time producing than performing. I love playing DJ sets, and while I already have enough of my own material prepared to develop a full live show, the right opportunity has not yet presented itself. For the moment, Parissior’s music therefore appears mainly within my DJ sets. I have performed hybrid sets using hardware, but fees are sometimes so limited today that paying for additional luggage to transport equipment becomes impractical. The same applies to vinyl: I play vinyl locally, but when I travel, I usually perform with CDJs for exactly the same reason. Because of my day job, I only play around five or six gigs a year, and promoters generally approach me to perform DJ sets. However, I would definitely like to explore the live format when the right opportunity and conditions come along. About Parissior Parissior is the alias of Spanish DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. He began DJing professionally in his native Cantabria in 2001 under his own name, playing Techno and House. In 2004 he moved to Salamanca, where he became a resident DJ at venues including Cubic Club, Submarino and Beatz, and later opened his own venue, Clavel Ocho, whose upstairs floor, Espacio Cielo, was dedicated to electronic music. He started producing around 2004 and has released more than 600 tracks under various aliases. He created the Parissior alias in 2011 to explore Electro, Italo-Disco and EBM-influenced sounds beyond his earlier productions. Parissior has released singles and EPs since at least 2016, including “Could I Drown In Your Desire” and “Dance To The Groove” (Spa In Disco), followed by “Let Them Dance” (Hot Digits Music, 2017) and further EPs and compilation appearances for Golden Soul Records. From “Back To Earth” (2020) onward he has worked mainly through Espacio Cielo, the label he revived from his former venue’s name, releasing further singles, EPs and compilation tracks including “Battle Cry” (2021), “Raver In The Booth” and “Full of Stars” (2023), and the Skylax release “Antennae” (2024). “Human Control”, Parissior’s first full-length album, was released on Espacio Cielo in collaboration with Mots Music. Side-Line reviewed the album in September 2026, describing it as a mix of Dark-Techno and EBM. This interview follows that review.
items._cn_summary: 西班牙艺术家Parissior（真名Jesu Aparicio）在专辑《Human Control》中探讨人与技术、控制之间的复杂关系。作品以暗黑电子声响为核心，融合EBM与工业元素，复刻1990年代法兰克福Techno场景的舞池律动，同时注入当代制作手法。从DJ转型制作人，艺术家将多年俱乐部经验注入作品，在暗潮氛围与身体律动之间取得平衡。专辑由其个人厂牌Espacio Cielo与Mots Music合作发行，属于独立地下厂牌范畴。作品概念清晰，主题紧扣当下技术社会议题，声响层面兼具压迫感与可舞性，为暗黑电子领域值得关注的年度新作。

items.body: Is Woven Ground an EP with an accompanying film, or a film with an accompanying EP? We’ll leave it to the project’s viewers and listeners and to decide. Either way, Blair Coron‘s multi-media release is a treat for the eyes and ears, a celebration of Scottish forests, islands and glens, filled with lush instrumentation, poetry and harmony, coupled with sumptuous landscapes and insightful interviews. As Coron explains, “I could never say, ‘This song is the river’ or ‘these words are the forest’ … so I took my instruments and recording equipment and friends to the places I was writing about.” The landscapes are first seen from a moving car, then the disembarking, revealing the sounds of the village and the port. In the early minutes, Coron celebrates the gift of the Isle of Canna, a sacred trust and sanctuary. The cows seem as relaxed as the strings and historical piano, or the other way around. The views are bucolic, the pace of life unhurried, the area seemingly free from pollution, time in suspension. The natural soundscape is allowed to take center stage (more detectable in the film than the EP). In the first interview, one learns of apple trees fertilized by the bodies of seals. Farmland equipment lies abandoned; an ancient church stands witness. Local residents express pride in their location and history. Shoes off, windows open, Coron engages with the piano; “Isle of Canna, Midsummer, 5:54am, 2026” arrives a third of the way into the film, but is the EP’s opening piece, a love letter to the location. The next piece takes a little more work; a harmonium is not an easy instrument to move, especially across uneven terrain. The sprightly “Sgùrr A’ Mhaoraich” is performed by a babbling brook, with Charlie Stewart on the much more portable fiddle. The piece is an ode to the countryside and the flowing water, whose music never ends. As the camera zooms in to the reel-to-reel, the recording device begins to look like a stream. Coron sits outdoors at a table, reciting “Beneath Six Black Poplar Trees,” a poem that looks back to the dawn of creation, with creation itself the accompaniment. His voice is comforting, with gentle inflection that matches the spider webs undulating in the wind. The strings return, setting up the gorgeous closer, which includes Miwa Nagato-Apthorp and Zoe Bestel on layered vocals. “Hymn,” while not on the EP, is one of the highlights of the film (35:12-38:06, a music video on its own). An adjacent version was released on the Two Old Songs EP in April, the original on On the Nature of Things, but we like this choral version the best. For “Moon Lament,” the quartet sits in the woods, captivated and captivating, having become part of the visual and sonic scenery, melting into the forest like the voices of the water and the wind. This ebullient song is chased by warm laughter and the twittering of birds; the camera draws back, revealing canopies of green. Woven Ground the EP becomes a souvenir of Woven Ground the film. The images resurface when playing the music, stored in the memory as the seeds are stored in the earth. (Richard Allen)

items._cn_summary: 这张作品模糊了EP与纪录片的边界，艺术家亲自携带乐器、录音设备和友人前往苏格兰的森林、岛屿与河谷进行实地创作。专辑将簧风琴、小提琴、人声与自然环境音融为一体，搭配诗歌朗诵和当地居民访谈，视觉与声音同步展开。多首作品在户外场景录制，如溪流旁的提琴演奏、林地中的四重唱人声，录音过程本身成为艺术实践的一部分。整体呈现出对苏格兰自然景观与社区文化的沉浸式致敬，是音乐与影像、声音与地点深度结合的跨界作品。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As a Japanese band, De Lorians, whether intentionally or not, approach the Canterbury scene from a unique angle. Their sound is more experimental, linking them to the musical anarchism of both Koenji Hyakkei and Frank Zappa. One could describe their musical direction as driven by a trio of instruments: guitar, saxophone, and keyboards. "Daytona" nods to all these influences, ranging from pure jazz to the classic Canterbury keyboard sound. By the time "Magso" begins, the mood darkens, evoking Soft Machine, complete with saxophone riffs that lend a Piazzolla-esque aura to the final mix. "A Ship of Mental Health" kicks off with dissonant, magnetic polyrhythms; psychedelia and jazz-rock blend together, as if in a cocktail shaker, until they become one, yet they aren't the only ingredients in the mix. There is a chaotic sense of humor, undoubtedly inherited from their "Rock in Opposition" and Zeuhl influences, with traces of Samla Mammas Manna evident. Free jazz and funk merge in a style reminiscent of Gong, and the quintet sounds incredibly tight and cohesive, without sacrificing any sense of freedom or freshness."Gomata" reaches new heights, driven by the keyboards, which truly open up new sonic vistas, while the saxophone weaves invisible threads in the background, enriching the sonic depth and setting the stage for Roccotsu to launch into a highly evocative brand of space rock; indeed, the uptempo funk of the keyboards and saxophone that follows is perfectly suited to giving this space-age psychedelia a fresh identity."Himalia" is one of the strangest and most interesting tracks; Genki Goto's bass, combined with a distorted keyboard that mimics a violin, gives it a sound reminiscent of the band Egg during their most frenetically intense moments."Toumai" captures the band's essence: a sophisticated, free-flowing jazz sensibility fused with distorted, experimental rock, driven by either guitar or keyboard, that streaks across the sky like a line, eventually connecting with another to form a rainbow (the kind that appears only when it rains and the sun shines simultaneously). Reconciling this apparent contradiction, the blend of sensibility and madness, may well be one of the keys to the Canterbury scene style we see here once again.
items._genre: Canterbury scene / experimental jazz-rock / avant-garde / psychedelic fusion
items._cn_summary: De Lorians是来自日本的Canterbury场景乐队，以吉他、萨克斯和键盘三重奏为核心展开实验性爵士摇滚。专辑融合自由爵士、放克、迷幻摇滚和Zeuhl摇滚反对运动等多种元素，呈现出兼具理性架构与混乱幽默的独特美学。作品中既有致敬Soft Machine和Gong的经典段落，也有借鉴Egg和Samla Mammas Manna的复杂节奏织体，键盘与萨克斯的互动尤其突出。乐队五人编制展现出高度默契，作品中实验性与可听性并存，兼具日系前卫摇滚的精致与西方爵士传统的即兴精神。整体而言，这是一张在传统Canterbury框架内注入东方视角与自由爵士精神的跨界实验作品。

items.body: Review by alainPP — This EP marks a period of reflection following the departure of two band members, including Charlie. So, is it a transition or an evolution?"In a Fever Dream" is a gentle, melancholic acoustic track with whispered vocals, a fragile sound that develops into atmospheric djent metal with thunderous riffs and trip-hop influences. The lyrics explore a sense of disorientation?a sign of things to come? The contrast with the drum polyrhythms and savage growls, the restrained, solemn crescendo, and the surprising Ross, is striking. "Delirium" features a piercing, syncopated riff over an industrial beat and a Haken-esque chorus. The djent element returns on this tightly packed, flawless track, culminating in an explosive, exhilarating outro that launches into "Eclipsed by You," a slow-tempo track that veers between staccato metallic vocals, a deafening groove, and progressive keyboard electronics. The track is linear and highly professional, a testament to the innovative nature of this song, which balances unbridled gentleness with restrained violence."Bleeding Sky" boasts a subtle, syncopated groove and the ever-present vocals, a hallmark of this band. An ambient break reminds us that HAKEN has a distinctly modern prog-djent metal signature with its hypnotic crescendo. The crackling pads give way to cinematic, bucolic bird sounds. "Lotus," with its ethereal piano, offers a gentle opening; a captivating, hypnotic sound with an oppressive groove. The djent guitar enters over Ross's distant, trembling growl. The alternation between the break and the long, atmospheric drift sounds like a fresco faded by time, lacking in ferocity, and Ross's falsetto reinforces this ethereal, post-rock feel.HAKEN returns to visceral, more technical prog-metal. A deceptively complex album, far more intricate than it initially appears.
items._cn_summary: 这张EP诞生于乐队两位核心成员离开之后，呈现出明显的过渡与反思色彩。作品从轻柔忧郁的原声吉他与呢喃人声开篇，逐渐延展为带有trip-hop影响的氛围化djent金属，雷霆般的失真 riff 与复杂鼓点节奏形成张力。曲目之间在克制庄严的渐强段落与爆发式失控之间反复切换，慢速曲目在断裂式金属唱腔与电子键盘音效间游走，平衡了温柔与暴力。专辑还融入环境音效、田野鸟鸣等电影化声景，后期作品回归技术性更强的前卫金属路线。整体编曲精密，表面旋律之下暗藏多层次结构复杂性，是一张伪装成旋律化作品的高密度实验性金属EP。

items.body: This is the second album from this Dutch project, released last year. The work comprises eight tracks that immerse the listener in an intense, almost archaic sonic experience. Noise, Industrial, and Dark-Ambient are fused into a powerful production that radiates terror. The heavily manipulated sounds and screaming vocals evoke the early magic of 1980s experimentation. While it could easily be categorized today as Power-Electronics or Death-Industrial, this is first and foremost an extreme record of lacerating sounds that will slice through your ears at high volume. This is not a record for the faint-hearted, but rather a sonic feast for connoisseurs of extreme musical experiences. (Rating:7). Listen to “No Good, No Evil”: No Good, No Evil by Spur On To XS About Spur On To XS Spur On To XS is a solo Noise and Power Electronics project based in Eindhoven, the Netherlands. Dunkelheit Produktionen released the project’s debut full-length, “Indulge In Primal Ecstasy”, on 22 September 2024 (catalog DP171CD). The label followed it with “Sacrifice As The Cornerstone Of Society” on 7 June 2025, issued as a handnumbered CD edition of 200 copies with a 4-page booklet alongside a digital edition; all eight tracks were written and recorded by Spur On To XS, with production credited to Dunkelheit Produktionen. The project also self-released the cassette “Adoration & Scorn” in 2025, and the cassette “Amphetamine Kommando” followed on Lust Tapes on 1 September 2026.
items._genre: power electronics / death-industrial / dark ambient / noise
items._cn_summary: 这是荷兰埃因霍温单人项目Spur On To XS的第二张专辑，包含八首作品，将噪音、工业与暗氛围融合为极具侵略性的听觉体验。大量处理后的声音素材与尖锐嘶吼人声交织，呈现出对1980年代早期实验音乐语境的追溯。整体制作强调高音量播放下的物理冲击感，声响设计以撕裂与切割为核心美学。评论将专辑定位为面向资深极端音乐爱好者的作品，而非普通听众。发行方面采用地下厂牌手工编号CD（限量200张）配合数字版本，延续了欧洲暗潮/工业场景的独立制作传统。

items.body:
A key presence on the New York scene over the past 30 years, trumpeter, composer, arranger, and bandleader Steven Bernstein has immersed himself in such a wide array of music with his bands Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Diaspora Soul, Universal Melody Brass Band, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and the Butler-Bernstein Hot 9 that his output defies easy categorization. A former member of The Lounge Lizards and Levon Helm’s Midnight Ramble Band, Bernstein has also composed works for film, theater, and dance in addition to doing arrangements for a diverse list of artists, including Lou Reed, Lee “Scratch” Perry, Allen Toussaint, Marianne Faithfull, Linda Ronstadt, Rufus Wainwright, Darlene Love, Mario Pavone, Bill Frisell, and John Lurie. His lengthy list of sideman credits includes appearances on recent recordings by Laurie Anderson (Heart of a Dog), Roswell Rudd (Trombone for Lovers), Mostly Other People Do the Killing (Loafer’s Hollow), Antony and the Johnsons (Turning), and Nels Cline (Lovers). He also continues to perform with Ray Anderson’s Pocket Brass Band, Omaha Diner, and the Kamikaze Ground Crew.

Born in Berkeley, California, Bernstein moved to New York in 1978. By 1990 he had joined The Lounge Lizards, appearing on the group’s 1991 release Live in Berlin (Intuition). Shortly before that, in 1988 he formed the trio Spanish Fly with slide guitarist Dave Tronzo and tuba virtuoso Marcus Rojas. By 1995, producer Hal Willner, a fan of Spanish Fly, enlisted Bernstein as arranger for the soundtrack to Robert Altman’s film Kansas City, which led to collaborations on numerous other Willner projects, including tributes to Bill Withers, Doc Pomus, and Leonard Cohen, among many others.

In 1996, Bernstein formed Sexmob with saxophonist Briggan Krauss, bassist Tony Scherr, and drummer Kenny Wollesen. It remains his primary vehicle for exploring the slide trumpet, a rare instrument that he picked up in a Woodstock guitar shop back in 1977. Over two decades of recording, the group has put their singular stamp on an eclectic list of tunes by the likes of Leadbelly, John Barry, Hoagy Carmichael, Paul McCartney, Duke Ellington, Prince, Kurt Cobain, the Rolling Stones, James Brown, Count Basie, Professor Longhair, and Nino Rota. The group’s latest album, in its 20th anniversary year, is Cultural Capital, the first Sexmob recording to feature all original compositions.

From 1999 to 2008, Bernstein contributed four recordings to John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label – 1999’s Diaspora Soul (featuring members of The Lounge Lizards and Sexmob), 2002’s Diaspora Blues (featuring Sam Rivers), 2004’s Diaspora Hollywood (inspired by classic film composers and West Coast cool jazz), and 2008’s Diaspora Suite (a homecoming recorded with Bay Area musicians). Each project combined traditional cantorial songs and elements of jazz, blues, and rock.

Bernstein’s Millennial Territory Orchestra debuted with 2006’s MTO, Vol. 1, which featured large ensemble interpretations of songs by Stevie Wonder, Prince, and the Grateful Dead, as well as Benny Moten and Charlie Johnson and His Paradise Band. They followed with 2008’s We Are MTO, which included renditions of tunes by Fats Waller, Don Redman, Count Basie, and the Beatles. Their 2011 recording, MTO Plays Sly, was a tribute to the music of Sly & The Family Stone and featured the late P-Funk keyboardist Bernie Worrell along with guest vocalists.

In 2012, Bernstein joined up with New Orleans piano master Henry Butler in the retro-flavored Butler, Bernstein and the Hot 9. Their critically acclaimed 2014 Impulse! debut, Viper’s Drag, featured spirited renditions of Fats Waller’s title track along with tunes by Jelly Roll Morton and originals by Butler. The restlessly creative Bernstein continues to juggle several working bands. During a recent residency at The Stone in NYC, he performed with Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and Universal Melody Brass Band.

Bernstein’s latest album is ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance (Royal Potato Family). In the liner notes, Bernstein mentions being enchanted by Burning Spear’s Garvey’s Ghost (Island, 1976) back in 1981, only realizing years later that it was a dub version of Marcus Garvey, Burning Spear’s Island release from the previous year. Since then, Bernstein has wanted to record an acoustic jazz trio album and have the results remade as a dub album. The first half of the release, ResoNation Trio, features Bernstein on trumpets, Scott Colley on contrabass, and Nasheet Waits on drums. To challenge himself, Bernstein eschews his main axe (slide trumpet) for this session and instead plays regular valve trumpet, G trumpet, and flugelhorn. The second half is called Ultra Resonance and features the first session tapes remixed and rearranged in dub fashion by longtime producer Scotty Hard, who also adds various keyboards, samples, and percussion to the mix. The former date is as spartan as the latter is dense, yet the two recordings (different though they are in concept and execution), are inextricably linked. I interviewed Bernstein in the summer of 2026, shortly after the release of ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance.

* * *

Troy Collins: You’ve been touring with Laurie Anderson the past few years, as documented by the recently released Let X = X (Nonesuch), which features Sexmob as Anderson’s backing band. What has it been like interpreting and rearranging her tunes for Sexmob, especially since Sexmob (in)famously doesn’t typically use pre-arranged tunes and/or setlists? And perhaps more importantly, how did this particular collaboration come about and what is working with Anderson herself like?

Steven Bernstein: Playing with Laurie has been a life-changing experience. She is completely about creation, being in the moment, acting on every inspiration, trying every idea and having fun. Her work ethic is legendary. Her ability to transform an audience is mastery. So being around her and that energy is just a powerful and positive situation. Even though a “show” is basically set once Laurie has decided on it (we are touring a completely different concert, different songs, different stories, different visuals, and a different “theme”) we/she are constantly making changes. Every show day we are at the theatre by 2:00 pm (she gets there at 11:00 am to start working with the lighting director) and we run every piece, whether a new idea comes from Laurie, me, another member of the band, a random sound that makes Laurie say “What’s that? Let’s try that in ‘___’.” Every idea is entertained and often added to the show.

The story of how this all started is beautiful. I’ve been around Laurie and known her at a distance for a long time, but the first time we really worked closely was doing Hal Willner’s Leonard Cohen show in Brighton in 2004. I arranged two songs for her, “The Guest” and “If It Be Your Will.” At Hal’s memorial she wanted to do Lou Reed’s “Gassed and Stoked.” I brought an arrangement that sounded just like the record and we played it through. She turned to me and said, “that sounds great, but I had another idea, I have this new loop” and she starts activating the loop with her violin bowing. It was a very “Laurie-style” loop: rhythmic, sonic, and not in 4/4 time. Tony and Kenny just drop in and start playing. It was grooving and effortless from the first sound. Laurie ended up testing positive for Covid and was unable to play the memorial, but a week later she calls and says how much fun she had playing with us. She said, “I’ve never had that feeling playing music” and that Warners is re-releasing her records and she was thinking of revisiting her older material (which she had never done), and asked would Sexmob play with her? You know my answer.

TC: Since you mentioned him, I’d be remiss to not ask about your years working with Hal Willner. The man’s various artist projects were significant touchstones in my development as a listener. I know he was a big fan of Spanish Fly – is that how you first met? And how did you become his go-to arranger for so many of his projects?

SB: I heard Hal’s Nino Rota record the summer of 1981 while visiting back home in Berkeley. Peter Engelhart, the legendary metal percussion maker played it for me (his daughters are some of my oldest and best friends). It changed my DNA! After that it became a thing. Who is Hal Willner? Where is Hal Willner? I did Night Music with Karen Mantler in 1989. I also played with Carla Bley, Bootsy, and Allen Toussaint on that show. Hal came up to me and said that he was a fan of Spanish Fly, that he’d been coming to our gigs at the Knitting Factory (lurking in the back I’m sure). He gave me his number and said that he would love to help us in any way he could. That led to him producing the first Spanish Fly record (on Knitting Factory records). It is a great Hal Willner production. Hal and I had very similar musical loves and ideas about music, he believed in me and kept offering me amazing opportunities. That led to a 25-year relationship. He could ask me to arrange for Elton John, Bill Frisell, Nick Cave, Lou Reed, Courtney Love, Robert Altman, Marshall Allan, U2 – it was always magic and natural. When I met him, it was pre-internet, and I would keep a pad of paper next to me during our phone conversations. His references could be Ernie Kovacs, Rahsaan, Allan Ginsberg, Martin Denny, Dorothy Parker, Anne Waldman, The Three Stooges, Gregory Corso, Fellini ... I did my best to keep up and learned a lot.

TC: Talking about Willner reminds me that you’ve done arrangements for more people than I can list, and the stylistic variety of artists is staggering. I’m curious if there’s ever been any job you feel you couldn’t or wouldn’t do?

To clarify, the beautiful thing about music is that someone else can take a song that seems unsalvageable and make something new from it that the original author may not have ever suspected was possible. Having just listened to a recent interview with Bill Frisell, I was reminded of his rendition of Madonna’s “Live To Tell,” which transforms what I would consider to be a lightweight pop song into a rhapsodic epic.

You are obviously capable of the same magic, but I wonder, have there ever been offers that you’ve refused based on the material or direction that someone wanted to go with it? Have you ever encountered a song that you felt was simply unredeemable?

SB: Well, there’s a funny story from about 8 years ago, at the beginning of Trump’s 1st term. It was a slow time (as often is the case for freelance workers) and I got an email from someone about arranging/producing some songs. The guy is a Sexmob fan, knows my work with Hal, and he has written some protest songs, tells me he thinks he can get Bono to sing on them, etc. He is not a professional musician, but this is his passion. He also has a vision of a performance piece situation, where the song is played while the listener goes down the “golden elevator” and walks somewhere else. We agree to a fee and he sends me the demo. He is playing rudimentary chords on the piano, and sings one verse, one chorus – it’s about 25 seconds. I call him and ask if there is more, he says no that’s the song. I explain that songs usually have a second or third verse, maybe a bridge, but he says no this is the song. I explain to him that it’s about 25 seconds, and if he wants it to work the way he is envisioning, (going down the elevator and walking) it needs to be at least 3 minutes long. He says, “Well do that Sexmob thing.” I talk to my wife and tell her that I don’t know if I can do this and she says “I thought you said you can make music out of anything.” So, I did and it ended up very cool!

TC: Well then, the obvious follow-up question to that is – did Bono sing on it?

SB: NO. A total pipe dream!

TC: Since we’ve been talking about arranging, I assume nothing is off limits in your own bands regarding your original tunes. Are there any pieces specifically written for say Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, or Spanish Fly that don’t translate as well from one band to the other, or do you compose your pieces so that any of your bands can perform them?

SB: Each piece is written not only for the band, but specifically for the players in each band. So, there hasn’t been much crossover. There is a piece I wrote as a commission during the pandemic that I played with Sexmob and MTO, but it really worked better as an MTO piece. But the very last phrase (the kicker) of the MTO end of night theme came from a Spanish Fly composition!

TC: Let’s move on to your new album. Your latest release for Royal Potato Family, ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance present two very different facets of your artistry – the former title finds you playing on valve trumpet and flugelhorn (instead of the ubiquitous slide trumpet) accompanied by bassist Scott Colley and drummer Nasheet Waits, while the later features Scotty Hard remixing the trio. How did this project come about and when did you first meet and work with Scotty Hard? It seems to me your working relationship with Hard goes all the way back to the very first Sexmob album, 1998’s Din of Inequity.

SB: This project came about because of a grant from the Shifting Foundation. The idea of creating original music with the orchestration of valve trumpet, acoustic bass, and drum set has been a dream of mine for a very long time. This particular vibrational intersection is not widely used, so the unknown possibilities are vast. On a musical/improvisational/technical level it has a very specific set of challenges, and it has taken me this long to feel ready to undertake this long-held desire. Scott Colley and Nasheet were always the musicians I wanted to do this with; I have known them both a long time, and they are veteran masters of spontaneous composition. Another long-held dream has been to create a dub version of an improvisatory instrumental record. I heard Garvey’s Ghost in 1981, and it changed my DNA. Once I started making my own records, I was just waiting for the right opportunity ... and this was it. The trio record is purely conversational and in the moment; back porch music with unlimited harmonic and structural possibilities. The time spent on this record was the decades of playing and writing that preceded it. Ultra Resonance is a mirror image, in that Scott creates his pieces layer by layer, adding and subtracting sounds and rhythms – it takes weeks to build a track.

When I first started playing in The Lounge Lizards with Michael Blake on tenor, Scotty started coming to hang; he was a friend of Michael’s from Vancouver. The first session we did with him was for a Justin Warfield record on Quincy Jones’ label Qwest. It was produced by Prince Paul (I am a huge fan of De La Soul). Scotty wrote the horn chart and engineered. Scotty went on to record and produce the first four Sexmob records. I was already doing fast cuts and dropouts live, but Scotty’s mixes/arrangements shaped the sound of the band.

TC: Having just listened to Sexotica (Thirsty Ear, 2006), your collaborative effort with the production duo known as GoodandEvil (Danny Blume and Chris Castagno), I’m curious how that experience was compared to your similar efforts with Scotty Hard? How does GoodandEvil’s working method differ from Hard’s and what are your thoughts on the different outcomes?

SB: Regarding the two albums/processes – they were fundamentally different as working methods and outcomes. We went into Sexotica (which got a Grammy nomination) with the idea of creating a project that was half acoustic and half electronic. Sexmob went on and recorded all the compositions (two of them being loose jams with input from Danny Blume). Then we did a full day of overdubs with Kenny: wood percussion, metal percussion, bird whistles, and gongs. Then GoodandEvil did their magic. Some pieces skewed more acoustic, some more electronic. The idea was an even balance overall.

With Ultra Resonance Scott was given all the tracks (20 songs). The first track he made, “Titano,” was a piece that’s not on the trio record, but I felt it would be a good piece for Scotty to put his magic on. I figured he would do a “remix” of it, but he rewrote the bass line and created a brand-new piece (natch). After that it was just letting Scott experiment and follow his muse. We had mapped out a series of “zones” we wanted the pieces to be in, but everything Scotty created was totally unexpected. Part of this was the idea of intentional experimentation – on both of our parts. For me it was the idea of the acoustic record, for Scotty it was some new boxes/plug-ins that he had recently received, and the idea of not going back to his tried-and-true techniques. Also, with Sexotica I was not involved in their process, but with Scotty I would hang in the studio once the “track” was created, and was involved in arranging process (Scott claims I had 3 good ideas, I’d say more like 7.6).

As far as my thoughts on the outcomes – two singular recordings that I believe are unlike anything else in the modern recording world. I’m proud of that.

TC: Switching gears slightly (towards acoustic sounds), you’re a fan of vintage horns. I’m assuming that there are certain models you never take on tour and some that you take on the road more frequently? What are the criteria for those distinctions? And what about the slide trumpet? I’m not familiar with anyone else playing one, so where and when did you ever find one?

SB: Vintage trumpets aren’t an issue on the road. I just use the horn best suited for the music. The horn I used touring with Levon Helm was a handmade Chicago Benge from 1947. That was a horn that could project over a five-piece horn section and two electric guitars. It had amazing response and Levon could feel my beat matching his. That’s not what I need with Laurie Anderson!

Regarding the slide trumpet – I found my first horn in a guitar store in Woodstock in 1977 when I was attending Creative Music Studio. When I started Sexmob 30 years ago my old friend (and master repairman) Dick Akright in Oakland (who I met in 6th grade) built the horn I use. It’s one a kind! I’ve collected almost every brand of slide trumpet over the years, though they are not as playable as my horn.

The first horn was $25, at the time (mid-70s) and many trumpet players had one because they were cheap and easily available.

TC: Speaking of Levon Helm, what was it like working with Helm and how did that relationship come about?

SB: This is a long story. I knew Levon had been having “rent party” gigs at the barn. Tony Scherr had done some, and Erik Lawrence did as well. Levon was in danger of losing the barn, as this was a last-ditch attempt to raise some money and also make some music. Erik had invited me to play a few times, and there was a Saturday where I was available (I often did a wedding on Saturday, as I was raising a family, and those gigs paid the bills). Anyway, they mention a few songs Levon might want to do (no Band songs) and said come up early because we might rehearse. We got up there and Levon didn’t come out, so I sat with a boombox and learned a few more songs that Levon “might want to do.” It was a nice chill hang up there, and when it became clear that there was not going to be any rehearsing, I told Erik Lawrence “Don’t play what I play. You just play what you hear, and I’ll play what I hear.” That way we were both free to react to the music. We were playing with Olabelle, and Levon just walked up and got behind the drums. It was the most natural improvisation/spontaneous composition. Levon didn’t know my name, had never seen me before, just smiled at me and told me what he needed with his drum fills. It was magic, and in true Levon form, he put a song from that night on one of his CD’s. Pure improvisation – we had never met!

As far as working with him – it was some of the most magic, swinging, joyous, pure music I have ever had the opportunity to create. He taught me so much about playing in time, playing melody, playing directly from the heart to the people. He was as great and real and no bullshit and smart as you would think from his legendary status. And we had FUN. And he went from almost losing everything to winning three Grammys in eight years!

TC: Speaking of legendary performers, how did you meet pianist Henry Butler, and what was your working relationship with him like?

SB: Another long and beautiful story. In the summer of 1984, I was working with the Flying Karamazov Brothers. We spent two months doing a show at the Goodman Theater in Chicago, and then went on to do a second show at the Olympic Arts Festival in LA. When that was over, they invited me up to the Eugene Country Fair, a legendary hippie festival that was associated with Ken Kesey and the Grateful Dead family. When they asked if I’d like to join them on the Old Time New Age Chataqua tour, a traveling group of “New Vaudevillians” – musicians and environmental activists that toured small communities in the rural Northwest, camping out and putting on shows – that seemed like a better option than returning to my non-air-conditioned fifth story walk up apartment on 109th street in July.

Our first stop was our one actual “gig,” at the Vancouver Folk Festival, and we headed up there directly from the Eugene Country Fair, where we had been enjoying the kind of quality research one would associate with the Grateful Dead Community. As we entered the festival, I heard a sound I was not expecting at a folk festival – a piano player, playing and singing music that seemed like it was completely futuristic, and at the same time playing music that seemed to come from early pre-jazz America. I had never heard anything like this, and at first, I thought my ears and brain were still vibrating from my Country Fair adventures, but it was actually being played, and it was (a pre-Impulse records) Henry Butler. He completely changed my DNA and I became a fan, buying his records when they came out.

When the Kansas City soundtrack record came out on Verve records, it was a time of flowing money in the record business, CDs were selling, and I believe the Bertleman Family had bought the Verve company. In 1995 they organized a cross-country tour with the Joe Henderson Trio, Charlie Haden Quartet West, and the Kansas City All-Stars, which included many Verve artists. I was the musical director of a band that included David “Fathead” Newman, Don Byron, Nicholas Payton, Christian McBride, James Carter, Mark Whitfield, etc.

I had contracted the band but was unable to find a piano player (Gerri Allen and Cyrus Chesnut had done the movie). I contacted seemingly every pianist in NYC who would fit the bill, and none were available, and I was starting to panic. I called Hal Willner to ask his advice and without missing a beat he said “did you call Henry Butler?” And that’s how it all started.

Henry and I were kindred spirits and when the tour was over he told me we would work together again. In 2011 I was doing an “MTO Plays the Early Blues” concert at a summer series in NYC. The promoter, Jay Weisman, asked if I’d like to have Henry Butler play, and I said of course, but where is he? It turned out he had an apartment in Brooklyn, post Katrina. When the concert was over Henry called me and said we should do a show with MTO playing all of his music – that was the birth of Butler Bernstein and the Hot 9 (there were 10 people in the band). As far as my working relationship, he totally trusted my bandleading instincts and arranging, and I was always awed and inspired by the music flowing out of him.

TC: You bring up a salient point. Around the time of the Kansas City soundtrack, there seemed to be a very healthy major label interest in jazz that benefitted musicians of all stripes, even those somewhat on the fringe (James Carter, Don Byron, David Murray, etc.), which to me, evoked the pre-Young Lions era, when major labels signed post-loft jazz artists like Anthony Braxton, Arthur Blythe, and Henry Threadgill.

Much has changed since then. I’m curious what your thoughts are on that phenomenon? How have you adapted to the changing fortunes of the recording business? And what do you foresee for the future?

SB: Well, the beautiful thing is that I have been DIY since the beginning. I think the budget of the first Spanish Fly record (which was on Knitting Factory Records) was 3K, and Hal Willner produced it! I personally have never really had a record contract where I was signed and had a budget. I’ve had a few independent contracts, and records funded by public and private grants. That is the way everything is now, so it’s just the way I’ve always been able to create new things. And that’s what it’s about, creating new things.

TC: In reference to creating new things, I’m curious about your thoughts on live performance versus studio recording. Studio recordings of Sexmob often feature a fair amount of electronic manipulation and remixing, much like Ultra Resonance. What are your thoughts on the difference between purely acoustic performances versus such heavily processed and studio manipulated recordings? Do you vary your approach towards playing depending on the situation?

SB: My feeling is that once Electric Ladyland and The White Album came out, there was no turning back. Even my albums that aren’t “heavily electronically processed” (aka produced by Scotty Hard) feature mixes that are very specific, often times emphasizing certain frequencies, the same way a painter will use certain colors to draw the eye. I believe a record should be a mind-altering listening experience. ResoNation Trio is also a studio record, although one that creates a vision of an imagined acoustic experience. As far as playing, I just do the best I can when the recording light is on!

TC: Let’s go back to those early, heady days. According to your bio, you grew up in the Berkeley area and were friends with Peter Apfelbaum, with whom you regularly attended jazz gigs. There was mention of an “eye-opening gig” by the Art Ensemble of Chicago at San Francisco’s Great American Music Hall. What was it about that particular show that resonated with you?

SB: It was just seeing them live after listening to the records for two years. The magic and visceral-ness of it. There is magic that happens when you are in the room, seeing the musicians and feeling the vibrations, sharing the communion of music. We also met them that night. We were pretty heady. We went to their dressing room and banged out “Nfamoudou-Boudougou” on the door. They were certainly shocked to open the door and see two scruffy teenagers.

They welcomed Peter and me into the dressing room, and that started a relationship that continues to this day (Peter is still in touch with Roscoe). When I moved to NYC I went to see the AEC at the Public Theatre, either late 1979 or early 1980. Now when we went to shows in the Bay Area everyone was dressed hippie funky, so that’s how I showed up, probably in overalls and a t-shirt. I go backstage after the show and am totally self-conscious to be surrounded by well-dressed urban New Yorkers in Kente Cloth and immaculate jewelry. Lester opens up the dressing room door, peeks out at all the “beautiful people” and says “BERNSTEIN get in here!” closes the door, points to the table and says “you can roll a joint, right?” (I could).

TC: Now that’s funny. I certainly remember my one and only time seeing the Art Ensemble of Chicago. It was in Philadelphia, at The Clef Club. Jarman wasn’t touring with them at this point, but it was still magical, ceremonial even.

One group I regretfully never saw was The Lounge Lizards. You were a member of The Lounge Lizards in the 1990s. How did that association come about? And while bandleader John Lurie has had an unusual (to say the least) life and career path since then, I was wondering, do you still have any contact with him?

SB: I have yet another tall tale to tell. It was summer of 1989 and I was touring with Chautauqua again, the same group of people I was touring with when I first heard Henry Butler in 1984. Back then we had answering machines that you called into and used a beeper to retrieve your messages (This is pre cell phones). I was in a small town somewhere, probably Idaho or Montana, and I went to a payphone and checked my messages, and I heard a message from John’s assistant saying to call John up because he was interested in having me join The Lounge Lizards. Needless to say I was beyond excited, because The Lounge Lizards was the “Premiere Band” on the downtown scene.

I call John up and the first thing he says to me is “Do you have a suit?” The next thing he says to me is “you’re not gonna get a lot of solos.” Luckily, the tour was heading to a place of general civilization (Port Townsend) and I was able to put together a tape so John had an idea of what my playing was like, and that September I started rehearsing with the band.

I still talk with John. The most recent project we did together was working on music for his film, that was two summers ago. We did music for Painting with John, and there was an excellent and entertaining episode in season three (I believe) that featured the making of the soundtrack, which really showed the process that we use.

Early on with The Lounge Lizards I started to arrange and transcribe for John, first working on Fishing with John, which led to arranging and conducting soundtracks such as Get Shorty and Excess Baggage. Get Shorty was the summer of 1995, and John and I would spend 12 hours a day together as I transcribed his ideas and put them into notated forms.

TC: I’m glad to hear you’re still in contact with John. Speaking of the 1990s, you recorded four albums in the late 1990s to early 2000s for John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label: Diaspora Soul (1999); Diaspora Blues (2002); Diaspora Hollywood (2004); and Diaspora Suite (2008). As a fan of those albums, I’m curious if you ever return to any of those tunes or arrangements?

SB: I’m glad you brought up those records. I love the Diaspora series too. Yes, it lives on. I wrote big band arrangements of some of this music for Arturo O’Farril and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra for two different concerts. I arranged a version of “Ani Mamin,” which I recorded with saxophones and valve trumpet on Diaspora Soul, reimagined as a tribute to Eddie Palmer and Conjunto Libre, arranged now for four trombones and slide trumpet. I learned that Barry Rogers, the architect of the New York salsa trombone sound, was raised in Brooklyn and his father and uncle sang with Moshe Kousevvitskey’s choir. Full circle New York history for you. I also recorded a version of “Cha” with Arturo and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra. We recorded it during the pandemic, so it's all over-dubbed. “Cha” was inspired by John Zorn’s composing for Masada, and I created an arrangement inspired by Machito. I recently revisited the Diaspora Blues music alongside Arturo O’Farrill, Anat Cohen, and a small version of the Afro Latin Jazz Ensemble. This October at the Stone I'll be premiering a duo version of the Diaspora music with Arturo O’Farrill, so the music lives on, and keeps evolving.

TC: What other musical projects or performances do you have coming up in the near future?

SB: Here are a few upcoming shows:

September 23-29: Laurie Anderson and Sexmob, West Coast Tour and Chicago October 1: Helm Family Ramble in Brooklyn October 2: ResoNation Trio at Tempo, Kingston NY October 28: ResoNation Trio at The Stone October 29: Ultra Resonance at The Stone October 30: Diaspora Special Edition with Arturo O’Farrill at The Stone October 31: Sexmob Kurt Weill Halloween at The Stone

Sexmob Live at Carambolage, Bolzano (the last night of our March 2026 European tour) will be released at the end of the year. It’s our first documentation of the “new sound” of the band with Kenny’s electro drums in the mix.

And more upcoming projects that I’m not quite ready to announce.

items._cn_summary: Steven Bernstein 是纽约实验场景中一位难以归类的多产音乐人，横跨爵士、犹太传统、布鲁斯、放克、电影配乐与流行改编等多个领域。他擅长使用稀有的滑音小号，在 Sexmob 等乐队中以独到的器乐语汇重塑 Leadbelly、Prince、滚石等人作品。Bernstein 长期参与 John Zorn 的「Radical Jewish Culture」系列，将传统犹太祈祷歌曲与爵士、放克、摇滚相融合，形成跨越文化边界的独特声响。作为 Lounge Lizards 前成员，他还与 Lou Reed、Lee "Scratch" Perry、Bill Frisell 等艺术家合作，并在 Robert Altman 电影《Kansas City》中担任编曲。其最新专辑《Cultural Capital》是 Sexmob 首张全原创作品集，体现二十年乐队积淀后的创作转向。整体展现了纽约下城跨流派即兴文化的多样面貌。

items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.

items._cn_summary: Ran Blake与Dominique Eade合作的专辑展现了高度个人化的艺术方法。Blake以独特的选曲逻辑著称，将看似毫无关联的作品并置，如Max Roach的《Mendacity》与《Saving All My Love for You》并列，揭示出隐藏的联系与深层结构，使熟悉材料呈现全新的面貌。Eade的声乐处理区别于此前与Blake合作的歌手，她不拘泥于Billie Holiday式的根脉，也不追求Sara Serpa式的克制内敛，而是以逐音节雕琢的方式诠释歌曲，在Whitney Houston流行热门甚至Mingus的《Portrait》等阴郁作品中都洋溢着鲜明的歌唱愉悦感。这种深沉喜悦成为她亲和力与作品感染力的核心，为Blake以钢琴为主导的非正统曲目编排注入了人声维度。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.
items.label: Artist release
items._genre: folk classical fusion / Slovak traditional / contemporary classical
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由小提琴家Ján Kružliak Jr.主导，汇聚三组音乐力量：弦乐四重奏Spectrum Quartett、传统民间小提琴组合Nogaband，以及女声合唱团Ulijanky，试图重建斯洛伐克古典作曲家与乡村民间音乐之间的历史纽带。曲目主要取材于Eugen Suchoň、Ilja Zeljenka、Alexander Moyzes及Bartók等作曲家从斯洛伐克民间采集素材后创作的作品，每首曲目的注释中都标明采样来源的音乐人与村庄地点。演奏与演唱充满原始活力，保留传统民间演唱的音色质感，拒绝管弦乐式的柔化处理，呈现出对民间传统深刻理解后的音乐呈现。整体呈现出斯洛伐克本土古典与民间传统的对话与重逢。
