items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以约两万名被俄罗斯强制带离乌克兰东部的儿童为题材，将传统乌克兰民歌与原创作品交织。Marichka与Alina Kuzma分别在加拿大和乌克兰集结女性音乐人，以弓弦乐器、班杜拉琴和钢琴为骨架，部分段落加入陶笛。歌词文本源于传统离别歌曲，既指涉历史上远赴异乡做工的少女，也映射当下被劫掠儿童的命运。乐评人刻意先不听说明文字、直接以声音切入，指出其音乐与人声在乌克兰本土标准之下同样扎实；阅读歌词后才意识到题材的分量。作品聚焦被占领土上的人道议题，音乐语汇以人声为核心，情感浓度较高，配器相对克制。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这是Bongo Joe厂牌发行的圣多美和普林西比70-80年代音乐合辑第二卷。乐评将Puxa描述为一种融合Merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等多种节奏的复合型非洲葡语区舞蹈音乐，葡萄牙殖民者曾试图禁止这种召唤或驱赶灵体的舞蹈形式但以失败告终。文章特别指出，由于圣多美只有12个村庄、缺乏大城市级别的录音工业，这种充满感染力的舞蹈音乐比实际规模所暗示的更加丰富。合辑收录15首作品，展现多把吉他相互交织盘旋、主唱与和声构成旋律框架的编制，Pedro Lima带领的乐队以闷音吉他和鼓组的对话为亮点，Africa Negra的曲目则呈现出延伸到数小时的现场感律动。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio
items.label: Taragot
items._cn_summary: 挪威Camilla Hole Trio的新专辑《Langs》在延续前作科幻合成器探索的基础上回归更为脚踏实地的声音，但仍将目光投向本国之外的民谣素材。主奏乐器高音萨克斯带来爵士语汇，开篇曲目《Springleik》取材于挪威西部传统舞蹈音乐，Egil Kalman的低音提琴与Knut Kvifte Nesheim的鼓构成节奏基底，而Kalman的模块化合成器与Nesheim的颤音琴叠加为音色增色。三人角色并非固定，旋律在萨克斯与贝斯之间交接，节奏不断展开，最终以即兴方式收束。整体呈现出传统挪威民间旋律与爵士即兴、实验音色之间的有机对话，乐器配置精简却层次丰富。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Hermidgets, the anonymous Italian dark synthpop project, has released “Like Moths” alongside an official video. The single is out now through Bandcamp and is the fourth preview of Hermidgets’ third album, expected in early 2027. “Like Moths” was mixed by Matteo Sandri and mastered by Giovanni Versari. A bass-heavy opening gives way to rhythmic, buzzing synthesizers, with Hermidgets’ baritone vocal set against a danceable groove and a bright, wiry synth line that recurs through the track. The lyrics follow two people drawn into a relationship whose destructive pull has become part of its appeal, turning surrender into something close to devotional: “Learn how to pray for the pleasure of having nothing.” The video, directed around a concept developed independently of the song, was inspired by French artist Olivier de Sagazan. Shot in black and white, it isolates Hermidgets’ head and shoulders as white modeling clay obscures and distorts his features throughout the performance, with black pigment introduced later in the video. The project keeps its members unidentified, and the clay imagery extends that approach by withholding a clear view of the performer’s face. Like Moths by Hermidgets About Hermidgets Hermidgets is an Italian electronic project that does not identify its members, combining distorted synthpop and darkwave songwriting with self-produced visuals. The debut album, “The Mire,” was released in November 2020 and included the songs “This Is Over” and “Nothing’s Perfect.” The singles “A Flaw” and “Perks” followed in 2021, and “Meaninglessness” and “We Tend to Disappear” appeared on the mini-album “NIHIL” in June 2024, recorded with a limited setup of two analog synthesizers, drum samples and voice. Hermidgets began previewing a third album with the single “Fall Apart” in July 2025, followed by “Sundown” in December 2025 and “Could I Be Better” in March 2026, a song that revisits “Could Be Better” from the 2020 debut. “Like Moths,” released in September 2026, is the fourth single from that album cycle, with the full album expected in early 2027.
items._cn_summary: 意大利匿名项目 Hermidgets 释出单曲《Like Moths》，作为其第三张专辑的第四首先行单曲，专辑预计于2027年初发行。音乐以低频厚重的贝斯开篇，随后切入节奏化的嗡鸣合成器声部，男中音人声搭配可舞动的律动与一条明亮而尖锐的合成器旋律线贯穿全曲。歌词围绕两人被一段带有自我毁灭吸引力的关系所牵引展开，将屈服转化为近乎虔诚的姿态。MV由受法国艺术家 Olivier de Sagazan 启发的概念独立发展而成，黑白影像中白色塑形黏土不断遮盖与扭曲表演者的面部特征，后期引入黑色颜料，强化了项目一贯隐匿成员身份的美学策略。整体制作由 Matteo Sandri 混音、Giovanni Versari 母带处理，延续了项目以两台模拟合成器、鼓采样与人声为核心的极简创作框架。

items.body: Susanne Jonsson and Jan Strandqvist of the Swedish band Red Mecca have returned after a hiatus. Their time away, however, was marked by intense and deeply painful experiences: Susanne’s sister was murdered and her relationship fell apart, while Jan struggled with addiction. Sometimes, nothing seems better than returning to creative expression—in their case, by making a new album. This record clearly holds great significance for them, even though the music remains true to Red Mecca’s signature sound and style. It is a polished album, balancing understated, sensitive, and refined tracks with a somewhat ‘harder’ Synth-Pop style. The songs are expertly crafted and beautifully sung by Susanne Jonsson, a vocalist who has nothing left to prove. Personally, I prefer their Electro-Pop style—which occasionally hints at EBM elements—as it really showcases their talent for creating great music. While some tracks may lack a definitive climax, I believe the choice to create a more restrained work was deliberate. This may not be my favorite album by the duo, but it stands as a significant and healing production in their career. (Rating:7½). Listen to “I’m On The Outside”: I’m On The Outside by Red Mecca About Red Mecca Red Mecca was set up by Jan Strandqvist, originally with vocalist Frida Madeleine, who left after four albums and was replaced by Susanne Jonsson. The Swedish duo released “Truth” in 2019, followed by the albums “Away” (2021) and “Stay” (2023), all on Massproduktion. Strandqvist discussed the band’s history, including a 2016 Swedish Manifest Award win and a soundtrack placement on “Killing Eve”, in a 2021 Side-Line Click Interview.
items._cn_summary: 瑞典双人组Red Mecca在经历成员丧亲、关系破裂及药物成瘾等重创后，以回归创作的方式完成了这张具有疗愈意义的专辑。整体延续了他们标志性的细腻合成器流行风格，编曲精致克制，歌手Susanne Jonsson的演唱沉稳且富有表现力。专辑在抒情化的低调曲目与更具冲击力的合成器流行作品之间取得平衡，部分曲目偶尔显现EBM元素的棱角。制作层面偏向内敛与自省，牺牲了一定的戏剧张力以换取情绪的真实感。这是一张承载个人创伤与重建过程的诚实作品，对于偏好暗潮与电子交叉领域的听众具备一定吸引力，但在声音实验性与类型突破上相对保守。

items.body: To celebrate and commemorate John Coltrane’s 100 th birthday, drummer extraordinaire Don Berman will reprise at the Chapel Performance Space in Seattle his original composition, 'Ascension Northwest', written in the spirit of Coltrane’s Ascension (Impulse!, 1966). As in the original, Berman has11 musicians playing a series of mantras interspersed with spirited soloing over improvised support from subsets of other players, including a double-bass duet. A preview of this year’s performance written by Paul Rauch appears in Seattle’s Earshot Jazz magazine: https://online.fliphtml5.com/risyt/Earshot_Jazz_09_2026/#p=13 You can hear earlier versions of 'Ascension Northwest' released here: https://threshold24.bandcamp.com/album/ascension‑northwest As a contribution for the FJB Coltrane birthday column, I’ve asked the 11 musicians performing 'Ascension Northwest' (myself included) to reflect on Coltrane’s Ascension and its impact on their musical journey. Below, our answers (gingerly edited). The questionnaire is reproduced at the very end. Tom Varner (French horn) 1. I knew about Coltrane and loved his music from his time with Miles, and also his ‘classic’ quartet recordings, when I was in high school and getting into jazz. I did not know about Ascension until a bit later, perhaps early in college. Even though I loved Ornette Coleman, and even Albert Ayler, I must say that very late Coltrane and Ascension was a bit :”Whoa! This is too heavy for me!” at first listen. I think I wanted to hear the ‘melodic line’ no matter how ‘out’ it was, and this music went beyond that. Eventually I grew to love it, letting go of the ‘I must hear a clear line’ worry and just enjoying being carried away in the power of the SOUND. I.e., that sound of a ‘scary but then NOT scary’ glorious totality of several improvisers all going full steam ahead at once. The JCOA Michael Mantler ‘Communications’ 3-LP set, from 1968, with Pharoah Sanders and other greats, was a kind of bridge for me to the world of Ascension . To a kind of ‘beautiful crying battle’ as opposed to just noise. Within one or two years, I was open to playing in those settings! 1a. Ascension opened up a new world of “multiple new sound-creating improvisers” creating new avenues that were not ‘just’ chord change or single-line orientated. From then on, Coltrane’s world and the worlds of, say, Xenakis and Ligeti, were not so far apart! 1b.Moving into the ‘90s, I worked with ensembles that had 6, 7, 8 winds with bass and drums. I was going for that high energy sound where it was ‘ok’ to not hear individual single lines and just get swept away in the sound. The best example of this is my own “Death at the Right Time,” on “The Mystery of Compassion” on Soul Note (1992). 5 saxes, three low brass, bass and drums. 1c. Ascension kind of gave us ‘permission’ to create beautiful and powerful structures with very little or no written music, just ideas, and trusting that the improvisers will create a lasting artwork on the spot. I love that! 2. This is very corny, but at age 18, I clearly remember thinking “Well, remember, Tom, if things get bad in the future, or very challenging, don’t forget to listen to Coltrane—that music is healing. That music will always be there.” And, I would also simply say, “thank you, Mr. Coltrane.” Jim Knodle (trumpet) I heard Ascension when it was released in 1966. I regard it as a companion to Ornette's double quartet project Free Jazz . The interaction between Scott LaFaro and Jimmy Garrison is really something! Perry Robinson told me that the whole thing started at the Federal Prison in Lexington where everyone practiced in the same room at the same time. They didn’t want them to rehearse, so they just played ad hoc . Kenny Mandell (alto sax) 1. I was probably 19 when I first heard Ascension . 1972 or so. Being in college, I had heard free jazz players in NYC, and I knew Sun Ra’s music. Ascension was way more organized than a lot of Sun Ra’s music insofar as it kept the traditional jazz form where there was thematic material followed by solos. There are motifs but there aren’t any chord changes to speak of, and there is some degree of cacophony. Depending on the player, some of the solos were more traditional, others were, I would say, divinely inspired, like Eric Dolphy’s. In my listening life at that time, I quickly went from Led Zeppelin to the Art Ensemble, Albert Ayler, Archie Shepp, and Cecil Taylor. Most people thought I was crazy. I related to the energy of it. The dissonance never bothered me per se. Ascension showed me that the big band format could be stretched. The rock stuff was relatively static in comparison. Hendrix was close. Everybody else stayed in the form. I see Ascension as important but not seminal. It’s certainly part of the canon. 1b. I’ve put many large groups together over the years. Part of the game plan for large group improvisation is to establish a level of trust. I’ve learned to pick people who are comfortable recognizing that the traditional limits or strictures put on playing are actually optional, and one can use or not use those depending on what sort of statement the whole piece wants to make. Murray Bookchin’s Post-Scarcity Anarchism (1971, 1986) was pivotal (early 1970s) for me as much as any of this music. I tried to use those principles in music and in organizing. My book some day will be called The Tyranny of Harmony . Piano chords in particular limit your choices as an improvisor. It’s also the case that as I’ve gotten older and found that the audience just hasn’t been there for totally unstructured, large-form music, I’ve tended to select pieces or write pieces that give the audience some sort of repeated motif to ground their listening experience. 1c. Ascension opened the door. After A Love Supreme (1965), people thought Coltrane took an extreme left turn into the world of sound exploration as it could be manifested in improvisation and group interaction. Ascension put into stark reality the challenges of making and of listening to that kind of music. I don’t think they got to the level that the Art Ensemble of Chicago did over the years, and some of Cecil’s groups that stayed together for years: Jimmy Lyons, Sirone, Andrew Cyrille, they practiced incessantly and got telepathic. 2. John Coltrane had an obsession with achieving a certain sound. Coltrane—his essence for me–is that ceaseless searching. This is what I love about music probably the most, it’s that it never ends. Dick Valentine (tenor sax) I reflected at length on the questions you posed, and on the evolution of my attitudes, responses and relations with Coltrane’s music, which I understand in a context of almost 60 years trying to educate myself and participate in contemporary expressions of Great Black Music. In the end, despite that his recorded output made a tremendous impact on my playing ‑‑ and was a singular factor in motivating my drive to make music ‑‑ I think it fair to say Ascension , the recording, has not occupied as big a space in my development or conceptualization as some other works. I played in Don Berman's three presentations of Ascension Northwest in 2016, and I'm very pleased indeed to get to do it again on the Coltrane centenary. I really cherish the privilege of participating with artists the caliber of those whom Don has persuaded. I look around the room at the assemblage of musical knowledge, emotional depth, technical proficiency, and aesthetic ambition, I am inspired and amazed and humbled. I’m long past accepting that I will never "understand" society. It seems to me the “order that governs power and human relations” in our real world is founded on out‑of‑date assumptions regarding what humanity needs to flourish. I know that there are many people aware of this damaging misalignment, and I can tell they mostly share my frustration that fixing large‑scale misalignments is not in the offing, thanks precisely to the systems that govern the distribution of power and dictate humans' relationship with real resources. So, on John Coltrane's centenary, we'll gather musicians, players and audience in celebration. In a sense, a roomful is perhaps a model of “society.” Everyone in the room will have some mental image of what constitutes a successful event ‑‑ in context, the definition of the community “flourishing,” right? As players, we have the responsibility to provide physical, audible inputs to the outcome. There is a bit of magic to what may happen here. Each player contributes to the global fabric, whose nature he may not predict. It’s understood that coordinated inputs are in some sense a prerequisite for success, and communication is required for coordination. How is communication achieved? By the act that constitutes that player’s input. It’s a bit recursive, to say the least! Neil Welch (tenor sax) 1. Ascension came my way when I was 15 or 16. I picked up the album in cd format at a record store. This was my first experience with Trane’s music on Impulse!. I picked up the album out of curiosity. I was initially struck by three things: 1. The album cover ‑‑ Coltrane the seeker, looking beyond himself, and beyond us to something cosmic. 2. The length of the album: Until this point, I didn't know that a ‘jazz’ album could be +/‑ 40 minutes in length. 3. The cd version had takes 1 and 2, which made it a double album. It was the most expensive CD I had ever bought. The response for me was immediate. I felt the album opened with a declarative question. Coltrane begins with a theme, but it is incomplete. The tonic is ‘missing’ from the first note he plays. He asks the band a question with only the partial theme, and leaves it to the band to complete that theme. Ascension felt to me a major and inevitable document in Coltrane’s music from this period. The emotional intensity of his solos, and what he was asking of a small group, had reached a tipping point. I found it deeply humbling and revealing that he used the vehicle of a communal sound to further amplify the concept of the jazz musician as soloist and group collaborator. 1a. After Ascension , I understood that in musical conversation, a powerful theme could be stated with brevity. A short theme can grant space for a complex response of virtually any length. 1b. Ascension helped me to experience song length as a durational mind-set. A song could, and ought to be, exactly the length needed to fulfill its musical and emotional aims. 1c .Ascension is, for me, an album of colliding forces and the unity of embracing those forces towards a common mission. It’s like people in a building. All these souls one floor atop the other. Different lives, worldviews, needs, hurts, wants, but all share the same vertical massing. If that building is on fire, they are invested in each other's outcome. They’ve looked in the eyes of those people in the elevator. 2. Can we as a society still sit with, and grapple with in real time, discordance in art‑making? Can intensity of sound and emotion hold space for us in our lives and aid us in the journey of deeper personal growth? Steve Meyer (alto sax) 1. I must have been 14 or 15. I was just getting into Coltrane and came across Ascension at my local record store. At that point I’d only known some of his earlier quartet work and work with Miles. Seeing that this was a larger group piqued my interest. And I recognized the names of a lot of heavy players, though I doubt I’d heard most of them at that point, so thought it would be a good album. After getting back home, I’m in my bedroom and put on the album. I don’t know what I was expecting but not too far into the first side (the first ensemble part) I knew it wasn’t for me. I didn’t know what to make of it, and it didn’t speak to me. I think I finished the first side but didn’t listen to the second. A few years went by before I was ready to give it another try. I was still an adventurous listener, so my first reaction didn’t turn me off from listening to other “out”/free musics which I grew to appreciate and enjoy more and more. 1a. If I don’t like what I hear on first listen, I remind myself that there are works of art out there that I’m not ready for. Music will speak to us when we’re ready to hear it. 1b. While I was listening to more out music in my teens it was years later before I played free music – at least with others. In high school this wasn’t the kind of music most of my musician friends would be into. Even with the one or two who weren’t opposed to it, we never thought to attempt it ourselves, at least not in any serious way, sticking to more standard jazz and the fusion music of the day. (This is early 80s, btw.) Even later, people I played with tended to be more conventional in the foundation of their music. These days I’m fortunate to have a community of musicians who embrace free/creative music. And, I have more confidence in myself to nudge the conversation that way when playing with others that I think will be receptive to it. 1c. I tend to not view music through a sociological lens, but Ascension and similar music has made me consider the normative orders of music in the US. Mainly, they’ve shown me there are a lot of stories to be told and a lot of different ways to tell them. 2. I want to thank Coltrane for his music and inspiration. The question to ask myself: how can I harness the focus and questing spirit of Trane? Eric Ring (piano) While A Love Supreme was life changing at 18, I’d surprisingly never heard Ascension prior to preparing for this performance. Don Berman (composer, drums ) 1. A sax player at my summer Maine resort job, a student of Jackie McLean, had introduced me to Coltrane’s Live at Birdland (Impulse!, 1964). This was 1972. I heard an amazing spiritual element in John Coltrane's music when I heard his quartet play “Alabama.” It struck me incredibly deeply and I have adored jazz and playing jazz ever since. (The piece was a deeply moving eulogy to the victims of bombing of the 16th street Baptist church in Birmingham, Alabama.) A couple of years later, in my junior year of college, I heard Ascension and realized that Trane had helped jazz expand its scope enormously to express a wider range of feelings. With the Ascension session, jazz composition and form had evolved light years from the beginnings of jazz decades earlier. After Ascension , there was now a huge universe of possibilities for jazz musicians to explore in their work. 1a.As I got further into jazz I particularly loved Miles Davis and John Coltrane, because I saw how each had evolved continuously throughout their musical journeys, from one period and chapter and style to another. The way I think about music and music making after Ascension is part and parcel of how I feel about music and art in general. All of the art forms have a rich and magical history. If you have studied and played music for years and years, you have to discover who you are and what your aesthetic is. 1b. For me, Ascension is part of what guided me further into freer playing and improvising in the last 20 years. Creating my own compositions has become more important for me. I organize pieces that contain both written and improvised sections. For this I select musicians that can both interpret written compositions and also improvise very well. 2. I would ask others: How does Coltrane’s music move you and make you feel about what feelings or sounds you play and express when you play? The world is full of a truly amazing variety of music. There are masters playing in each of those styles. I would ask others who take music seriously to open their minds and make sure they hear the music of master creators, live when possible, and in as many styles as possible. Master the basic fundamentals, and take music as seriously as Trane did. For those just seeking fun, that is fine too. A lot of striving people in the arts take things too seriously, especially when they become too self-absorbed and their egos interfere with what they are attempting to do as musicians. As the great pianist and educator Kenny Werner teaches his students and readers, “your value as a human being is not based upon how well you play a musical instrument.” Gregg Miller (baritone sax) 1. Around 1997 I bought a used CD copy of the compilation, The Major Works of John Coltrane (GRP Records, 1992) which included both takes of Ascension as well as Om , Kulu Se Mama , and Selflessness . I was stunned at the difference in intent between those recordings and Giant Steps . In Giant Steps , I heard a restless cramming of as many notes as quickly as possible within structures that could barely contain them. In Ascension , Coltrane had left that set of problems behind in favor of a compositional form that foregrounded the free-playing (and listening, or not listening) of every other player, a dense maelstrom that produced its own power without regard to or in opposition to or transcending of the traditional tropes of organized sound. To my ears, there was still an evident structuredness to the resultant noise, but full-on interplay was now the method and the lesson. It felt to me like a releasing of mutual respect, a lifting of repression inherent in most musics, and a deliberate shifting of power dynamics from a singular ordered mind that commands obedience (and players willingly, often reverently submitting to that control) to the shared embrace of others who jointly participate. Messy, but beautiful. I was studying a lot of Habermas at the time, and so for me, the link between music-making and communicative action was an easy one to see/hear and understand. I wasn’t playing free music (or any music) at the time, but the seed had been sown without me knowing it. 1a. In the late 1990s I would listen to Ascension and the other tracks on Major Works over and again while studying. It was the kind of music that permitted my mind to roam freely and/or easily concentrate elsewhere without demanding I enter its rhythms, melodies, cadence. There was something liberating in its power to shape time and experience like that. Among other things, it forced me to confront the limitations of pop music and its draw. 1b. As wild as Ascension s ometimes feels, it predicates without having arrived at a music that depends foremost on collective improvisation where listening and meaningful response have overtaken chops and strutting (not that chops and strutting can’t be part of meaningful communication). What opens up, then, is the possibility for music-making where the reception of one’s own and others’ sound while playing is governed by a feeling out of the pulse of the whole, accepting contingency and accident as integral to the flow of making. Musical “intention” in this context becomes an emergent property of the experience of intersubjectivity. 1c. Most (90%?) deliberately made music appears to our ears in strict time, where the musicians aim to become part of a single organism beating in time, and their music tries to compel listeners to imaginatively join that rhythmic organism. There is solace and belonging offered in that vision of unity and unfreedom. I’ve had enough of that music. How else might we imagine and experience collective practices of meaning-making/moving/sounding as individual and collective flourishing/belonging/being-with-others? Ascension. Questionnaire 1. When did you first hear Ascension, or come to know about it? What was your response? How did this event affect your understanding of Coltrane and what he’s up to, of jazz music, and/or music and what it’s up to? 1a. How do you think about music and music‑making after Ascension? 1b. Has Ascension (or its ilk) informed your practice – of playing, of organizing, of selecting musicians, of conceptualizing the field of music? 1c. Has Ascension informed your understanding of society, or, dare I say it, the normative order(s) that govern(s) our understanding of power and human relations? 2. What question would you want to ask of yourself, of others, about John Coltrane @100? Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 为纪念约翰·柯川诞辰一百周年，鼓手Don Berman在西雅图Chapel表演空间重新演绎其原创作品《Ascension Northwest》，以柯川1966年经典专辑《Ascension》的精神为根基。演出编制为11人，延续原作以咒语式动机串联独奏段落的结构，由部分乐手即兴支撑，并包含低音提琴二重奏段落。乐评以问卷形式收录了参演乐手的反思，法国号手Tom Varner回忆自己从高中时期接触柯川与Miles Davis合作及经典四重奏录音，到大学阶段才初次聆听《Ascension》时感到难以消化的经历，以及最终如何通过Michael Mantler的《Communications》三重黑胶套装作为桥梁，逐步进入多人即兴共存的声场世界。Varner谈到《Ascension》如何解放了多声部自由即兴的可能，使其在90年代探索六到八支管乐加低音和鼓的大型编制作品。整体文章兼具活动预告与艺术家自述色彩，但更接近集体口述史而非深度音乐评论。

items.body: Review by Second Life Syndrome — Originally written for theprogmind.comThe Emerald Dawn are back with Volume II of their epic, The Land, the Sea, the Air. The band has produced consistently, with increasing quality, over the past decade, and that continues here. This might be my favorite album from them (maybe second favorite after To Touch the Sky). Regardless, more people need to give them a shot.The Emerald Dawn comes to us from St. Ives, UK. They are four-strong, having the same lineup for the last seven years or so. The players are Ally Carter on guitars, soprano and tenor saxophones, and keyboards; Tree Stewart on vocals, keyboards, flute, handSonic, and Roli Seaboard; Dave Greenaway on 6-string bass, and Tom Jackson on drums.They play progressive rock that avoids the cliches. The songs are atmospheric and organic, not to mention quite lengthy. They sound like they could be straight out of the 70s, yet their sound is ever fresh to me simply because they don't really sound like anyone else. Their music is ethereal, mystical, spacious, and even a bit like a folk ritual at times.By now, everything about their sound is like comfort food for my soul: Ally's growling guitars, Tree's illustrious keys and flute, Dave's energetic bass, and Tom intricate drumming. There's a reason why all four of them end up in my top musician features every time they release an album: they are amazingly skilled players who value expression over technicality, authenticity over plasticity. And for my money? Tree has probably laid down the best keyboard performance of the year, swooning and flowing with clarity and majesty. All of the performances are incredible, though.The Land, the Sea, the Air (Vol II) follows the first volume from 2025, which I rather liked. But I think this one is stronger. It has only three songs, in true Emerald Dawn fashion. The first one is called 'Song of the Rainforest', which is twenty-one minutes long. And yet, it is one of my favorite songs by the band to this point. This lengthy instrumental piece is so atmospheric, but somehow also so groovy. The song pulls you into its foliage, and underneath those trees is plenty of searing synth, amazing sax segments, gorgeous melodies, and hypnotic portions that feel otherworldly. I particularly love the precious minutes towards the end that hover with smoky flute, like a spellbinding incense rich with emotion.The second track is 'Rivers of Tears', which is fifteen minutes long. This one took a little more time for me, but I've come to love the focus on piano. It has a bluesy, funk-oriented sound at times, and much of it is reserved and building towards something. The song is structured with more energetic portions in the middle and the end, and each half has its own character, one being piano expressions and the other being more sinister. It's a brilliant track.The final track is called 'Paradise', being about nine minutes long. And you know what? It's yet another favorite from the band. I can't get enough of it right now, actually. It's the most 'normal' song on the album, featuring great vocals from Tree, who also plays her cosmic heart out on the keys. Seriously, this track is both incredibly groovy, almost making me what to dance (almost), but the layers of keyboard melodies, the catchiness of the hook, and the final minutes of sheer instrumental glory are like celestial medicine for the mind. What a finish!The Emerald Dawn are seasoned musicians, yes, but they are passionate artists who truly feel the flow, taste the melody, visualize the color, hear the beating heart of it all. The Land, the Sea, the Air (Vol II) has some of their best work, both calming and foreboding at times. It is a balanced, well-written record that makes you want to start it over again as soon as it ends.

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Shifting from the brutal to the delicate within a single song - one of the hallmarks that Opeth handled with ease - reached a turning point with the groundbreaking "Damnation" (2003), an album that almost entirely dispenses with the hostile sounds of extreme metal to embrace the most melodic aspects of '70s progressive rock. A risky decision that, despite initial concerns, demonstrated the band's versatility in moving confidently between different musical styles, while leaving fans and critics alike wondering about the direction the band would take in the future.With "Ghost Reveries" (2005), their eighth album, the Swedes once again use death metal as one of the fundamental elements of their sound, integrated with progressive components that are far more developed than in their previous works. Mikael �kerfeldt's demonic growls, the monolithic and dense guitar riffs of Peter Lindgren and �kerfeldt - which evoke extreme bands like Morbid Angel, the more experimental Tool, or the classic Black Sabbath, among others - and a powerful instrumental foundation alternate and blend with deep, clean vocals, crystalline acoustic elements, and Per Wiberg's hypnotic and cosmic keyboards, to construct a sonic tapestry of contrasts and shifts in intensity that moves naturally between ferocity and a hypnotic, enveloping melancholy."Ghost of Perdition", "The Baying of the Hounds" - featuring evocative Jon Lord-style organ - and the oriental-inspired "Beneath the Mire" unfold across expansive instrumental valleys and peaks that showcase the band's maturity, and find their full expression in "Reverie / Harlequin Forest" - featuring superb clean and harmonic phrasing by �kerfeldt - and, above all, in the ritualistic and intriguing "The Grand Conjuration" - reminiscent at times of Pink Floyd's "Echoes" - the album's finest moments.And the influence of "Damnation" is also present and can be felt in the tremulous "Atonement" and "Hours of Wealth," with their keyboards and a certain jazzy flair, and in the closing "Isolation Years," with its acoustic and dreamlike character, featuring �kerfeldt's whispering vocals and Lindgren's arpeggios, ultimately shaping the excellent "Ghost Reveries", one of Opeth's finest albums and standing alongside the iconic "Still Life" and "Blackwater Park".4/4.5 stars

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑在极端金属与前卫摇滚之间架起桥梁，将死亡金属的咆哮、厚重的吉他riff与清澈的清嗓、键盘铺陈的宇宙感交织在一起。乐队在单首歌曲内频繁切换暴力与脆弱的段落，形成强烈的动态对比。曲目中既有东方色彩的器乐展开，也有爵士味和梦幻感的acoustic段落，Jon Lord式管风琴与Pink Floyd式的仪式感空间交替出现。整体制作延续了前作《Damnation》的内省气质，但重新将极端金属的强度纳入结构，呈现出更成熟的层次与情绪纵深。作为Opeth第八张专辑，它在类型融合的流畅度和细节编排上展现出高度的控制力，是乐队将多种风格融为一体的代表性作品。

items.body: Somewhere between the panic attack and the curtain call, Fiona’s Phobias have found a rather entertaining place to set up shop. Their six-track EP DEMOnS Vol. 1 dresses burnout, self-disgust, and impossible attachments in gothic metal, pop punk, and dark cabaret, with enough theatrical excess to suggest that the orchestra pit has opened directly into hell. The jokes have teeth, the guitars favor elaborate flourishes, and the people inside these songs keep discovering that their favorite distractions have become further reasons to worry. Formed in 2022, the project pairs the deliberately elusive Nikki L with vocalist Krisanna Marie, whose background includes Hatesex, Penis Flytrap, and burlesque fire Go-Go performance. Their own comparison of the working relationship to The Phantom of the Opera seems appropriate for music so fond of trapdoors and dramatic entrances. Marie’s ability to move from a knowing, almost conversational delivery into operatic gestures gives these elaborate arrangements a useful center: someone has to keep an eye on the audience while the scenery catches fire. Euphoria is Tragic starts with a chugging guitar figure planted between punk and metal, while Marie brings a retro rock directness to its catalogue of procrastination and depleted pleasure. Around the minute mark, the arrangement grows dense with baroque embellishment; a wiry solo takes on something of an electric violin’s bite. The bright momentum makes an effective companion to lyrics about getting bored with your own bad habits. “I feel my powers wane; a witch without her magic” supplies the perfect image for that particular exhaustion, when yesterday’s magnificent escape becomes today’s inability to answer an email. The theatrical scale expands on Play It Cool, which sets an almost lounge-like opening vocal against metal accents before breaking into a gallop. There is something of Malice Mizer’s baroque grandeur in the meeting of ornate arrangements and vocal melodrama, with the forward motion suggesting the carriage from Castlevania: Rondo of Blood racing toward Dracula’s front door. Beneath the spectacle lies a grimly familiar instruction: take your pill, eat your food, behave, and convince everyone that nothing is wrong. As Marie’s singing becomes more operatic, the pressure to appear composed turns increasingly sinister, eventually spilling into the song’s bloodied escape fantasy. Imaginary Sins brings piano, nimble bass, and busy drums into a crooked little cabaret before the heavier ornamentation takes over. Guitar flourishes answer the rhythm’s clipped figures, and goblin-like responses jostle Marie’s lead, as though every unwanted thought has secured a speaking part. Its funniest lyric finds the bodily absurdity inside a familiar wish: “Wishin’ I was pretty on the inside – But there’s just guts.” Jealousy, appetite, and self-absorption populate this ballroom of dancing demons, while the music’s constant activity makes obsession feel exhausting even at its most playful. The cover of Bang Bang, offered as an ode to Kill Bill, fits neatly among these accounts of love going horribly wrong. A Phantom-style organ opening and old-school metal guitar melody send the song toward the grand, charging territory of Bonnie Tyler’s Holding Out for a Hero. Its childhood games and adult abandonment acquire the dimensions of a stage tragedy, complete with an ornate guitar solo. Placed between the EP’s psychological grotesques, the familiar tune becomes another example of affection leaving somebody flat on the floor. Whispers and giallo-like synth tones introduce She Loves To Kiss That Doll, before sweeping guitars open the room around Marie’s voice. An operatic interlude, edged with chimes, suspends the heavier movement as she sings of attachment to a figure whose beauty depends on a terrible act of denial. Stuffing, cold hands, and the replacement of blood with a handsome face turn romantic idealization into physical horror. The return of the metal arrangement gives that revelation force, while the lyric’s eventual admission that he has long been dead makes the tenderness more disturbing than any decorative cobweb could manage. Closing track Bittersweet Darling begins with chilly piano and the worn texture of an old recording, then carries that melodic idea into a broad sweep of gothic guitar. Progressive tempo changes unsettle a romance conducted through black-and-white television images, broken mirrors, and the comfort of a boxed-up illusion. Its lover remains available because the screen can keep performing; the person watching has surrendered something harder to recover. By the final turn toward the knife and the closing credits, the song has brought the EP’s appetite for spectacle into uncomfortable proximity with self-destruction. Across DEMOnS Vol. 1, the sheer amount of decoration can crowd the stage, but Marie’s shifts in delivery and the songs’ sharply drawn situations keep the excess purposeful. Fiona’s Phobias are especially effective when a grotesque image exposes an ordinary humiliation: craving attention while avoiding people, mistaking possession for love, or spending all your energy on the thing that leaves you empty. They have given those contradictions a lavish production, and the casting department appears to have found plenty of monsters willing to sing. DEMOnS Vol. 1 is out now, released October 2 via Misophoniac Rabbit. Listen below and find the EP on Bandcamp and Spotify. items._cn_summary: Fiona's Phobias 的六曲EP将倦怠、自我厌恶与执念编织成一部哥特摇滚歌剧。乐队以哥特金属、流行朋克与黑暗歌舞剧为骨架，在繁复管弦化编曲中安排巴洛克式装饰与戏剧性转折。主唱 Evelyn 文在口语化低吟与歌剧化爆发间自如切换，为失控的声场维系叙事重心。曲目从朋克金属律动逐步滑入暗厅式的诡异歌舞剧，密集的吉他花奏与急促鼓组制造出强迫性思维般的音乐漩涡。歌词以自嘲笔法书写现代倦怠症候，将情绪崩溃转化为舞台化的逃亡幻想，荒诞中带有切肤的自省。整体呈现介于后朋克暗潮与戏剧化金属之间的实验性混合，适合追求另类剧场感的听众。

items.excerpt: エミル・パリジャン、タブラと交わる新作『Floating』 ヨーロッパジャズのソプラノサックス奏者として25年のキャリアを築いてきたエミル・パリジャンが、ACTレーベルから新作『Floating』をリリースした。ピアノのヤロン・ハーマン、ベースのリンダ・メイ・ハン・オー、そしてタブラ奏者プラブ・エドゥアールとの共演による本作は、古典音楽から世界音楽まで幅広い影響を吸収してきたパリジャンの語法が、非西洋の打楽器といかに対話するかを示す一枚だ。 France Musiqueのポッドキャストで語られた制作の背景によれば、この邂逅は偶発的なコラボレーションというより、長年培われてきた音楽的語彙の延長線上にあるという。ジャズがヨーロッパの文脈でどう自己更新を続けてきたか、その現在地を示す作品とも言えるだろう。 出典：https://www.radiofrance.fr/francemusique/podcasts/au-coeur-du-jazz/emile-parisien-6403447 コルトレーン生誕100年に、マルサリスとリーヴスが応えた新作 ジョン・コルトレーン生誕100周年を記念し

Musiqueのポッドキャストで語られた制作の背景によれば、この邂逅は偶発的なコラボレーションというより、長年培われてきた音楽的語彙の延長線上にあるという。ジャズがヨーロッパの文脈でどう自己更新を続けてきたか、その現在地を示す作品とも言えるだろう。 出典：https://www.radiofrance.fr/francemusique/podcasts/au-coeur-du-jazz/emile-parisien-6403447 コルトレーン生誕100年に、マルサリスとリーヴスが応えた新作 ジョン・コルトレーン生誕100周年を記念し、ブランフォード・マルサリス四重奏団とヴォーカリストのディアンヌ・リーヴスが、Blue Noteから新作『Dedicated To You』をリリースした。企画の出発点にあるのは、1963年の名盤『John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman』——テナーサックスとバラード・ヴォーカルという編成そのものを引き継ぎながら、長年の相棒であるピアニスト、ジョーイ・カルデラッツォらとの即興的なアレンジ作業を通じて、バラード解釈を更新したという。 生誕100年という節目に、過去の名盤をなぞるのではなく、その成り立ちに立ち返って新たな即興性を持ち込んだ点に、今回の企画の芯があるとも言える。既存の敬意の示し方とは異なる道を選んだ一枚として、聴き比べる価値がありそうだ。 出典：https://www.radiofrance.fr/francemusique/podcasts/au-coeur-du-jazz/branford-marsalis-quartet-dianne-reeves-eternellement-coltrane-8964069 ビートメイカー、キーファーがBlue Noteからデビュー ロサンゼルスのビート・カルチャーと結びつきの深いビートメイカー、キーファーが、名門Blue Noteから『Memory Bomb』と題したデビューアルバムをリリースした。ジャズとヒップホップ、ロサンゼルスのビート・カルチャーを融合させた作品で、ジャジーヒップホップの現在地を示す一枚として評されている。Blue Noteという老舗レーベルがビートメイカーの作品を迎え入れた背景について、今後の展開にも注視したい一作だ。 出典：https://glidemagazine.com/330465/kiefer-turns-jazz-hip-hop-and-l-a-beat-culture-into-blue-note-debut-titled-memory-bomb-album-review ニューオーリンズ、音と食が共存する理由 米国ニューオーリンズで、音楽と料理に関わる2人の共著による新刊『Rhythm & Roux』が出版された。著者のブライアン・ランドリーとピーター・ハリスは、著名なシェフと卓越した音楽家のコンビだ。 ニューオーリンズでは、音楽と食が別々の娯楽としてではなく、同じ場所・同じ共同体の記憶として息づいてきた。本書はその結びつきを、単なる郷土料理本としてではなく、ニューオーリンズの食と音楽がどのように共に進化してきたのかを描き出す。 出典：https://www.npr.org/2026/09/20/nx-s1-5940782/cookbook-rhythm-and-roux-brian-landry-peter-harris スティーヴィー・ワンダー『Songs in the Key of Life』の未発表曲を公開 スティーヴィー・ワンダーがアルバム『Songs in the Key of Life』の50周年を記念し、同アルバムの膨大なセッションから未発表曲を収録したEPをリリースした。 1976年にリリースされた『Songs in the Key of Life』は、スティーヴン・ワンダーに3度目のグラミー賞最優秀アルバム賞をもたらし、「I Wish」「Isn’t She Lovely」「As」「Sir Duke」といった現代のスタンダードナンバーを収録。ハービー・ハンコック、ジョージ・ベンソン、ミニー・リパートンなど多くのアーティストが参加している。 出典：https://pitchfork.com/story/stevie-wonder-unvaults-four-songs-in-the-key-of-life-tracks 今週すでにお伝えしたニュース 海野雅威がオスカー・ピーターソンの名盤『We Get Requests』に捧げるトリビュート公演を開催 【ジャズフェスカレンダー2026】10月／11月／12月開催のジャズフェスティバル＆イベント ロンドン発のアンチアルゴリズム音楽プラットフォーム「ROVR」─日本初のフェス&レコードフェアを新木場で開催 【石川紅奈｜インタビュー】“心の中の庭” で芽吹いた大切なものをあつめて─新アルバム『Garden』発表 投稿 【ARBAN WEEKLY｜今週の話題まとめ】キーファーがBlue Noteからデビュー／パリジャンとタブラの対話／スティービー・ワンダー名盤の未発表曲／ほか は ARBAN に最初に表示されました。

items._cn_summary: 本期周报汇总多条爵士乐坛动态。法国萨克斯手埃米尔·帕里西安与塔布拉鼓手合作的新专辑，展现欧洲爵士语境下非西方打击乐器的对话可能。布兰福德·马尔萨利斯四重奏与歌手戴安·李维斯合作，以《John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman》为起点重新演绎科尔曼诞辰百年主题。制作人基弗在Blue Note发行的首张专辑将爵士与嘻哈及洛杉矶街头文化结合。斯提威·汪德为《Songs in the Key of Life》50周年发布未发表曲目EP。此外还涉及新奥尔良音乐与料理文化交织的新书，以及多位日本乐坛演出与新专辑动态。整体偏向主流爵士体系内的回顾与延展，融合元素丰富但深度实验性有限。

items.album: The Sound of the Abbey
items.excerpt:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhyt
items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

(Interview)

Songbooks Live
(Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录十三支比利时乐团的作品，录制于1129年建成的帕克修道院，利用古老石质建筑的天然混响营造冥想氛围。曲目横跨多种风格：罗姆小提琴、弗拉门戈风手风琴bal-musette、阿拉伯乌德琴与地中海融合、鲁尔巴洛克风格曼陀林与羽管键琴合奏、单簧管独白、匈牙利Citera齐特琴配以喉音演唱与爵士贝斯，以及全即兴手风琴二重奏。专辑以宗教空间为灵感来源，十三位音乐家各自诠释对修道院石壁、回廊、千年蜜蜂等意象的理解，虽风格广泛却因共同的创作语境而保持内在统一性。由Bert Huysentruyt录制混音、Pieter De Wagter母带处理，整体音色温暖，呈现出欧洲世界音乐与室内乐交汇的独特面貌。

items.album: Les Crimes du Musette
items.artist: Dominique Cravic et les Primitifs du futur
items.excerpt:
Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds
items.body:
Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.
N'oublie pas Gr�co (excerpt)
A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, �The young have fire, but we have light.� In its own little corner,
Les Crimes du Musette
shines bright.
Tiny Sun -
Vanishment
(Review)
Carolina Chocolate Drops -
Genuine Negro Jig
(Review)

items._cn_summary: Dominique Cravic与Les Primitifs du futur的第五张专辑延续了他们自1986年以来的杂食传统。27首短曲穿梭于法国手风琴酒馆音乐、香颂、拉格泰姆、jug乐队与skiffle之间，乐器涵盖手风琴、班卓琴、尤克里里、口琴、锯琴乃至theremin。Cravic的念白式演唱带有Maurice Chevalier的平民气息，专辑既翻唱1925年的《Ukulele Lady》，也致敬2020年去世的法国抵抗运动歌手Juliette Gréco。整张专辑如同从阁楼中发掘78转唱片再以考古式的热情重新演绎，乐手多已年过七旬，但演奏态度严肃而投入。这种对被遗忘曲目的再激活带有强烈的复古趣味与世界音乐气质，但本质上仍属于怀旧型杂锦拼贴，创新性与实验性有限。

items.body:
I want to personally direct you to a remarkable piece of music titled "Two Views of a Prayer," composed and written by
David Dzubinski
as part of the
Prism Quartet
's new series of collaborations called
Unlocking Your Inner Composer
. If you have listened to my radio programs, you are probably familiar with the quartet's ground-breaking, genre-blurring music. If not, there's no better introduction than this.
Performed in November of 2025 at the Free Library of Philadelphia, they invited vocalist
Ursula Rucker
, percussionist
Tyshawn Sorey
, and violinist
Carlos Santiago
to collaborate on the arrangement and performance of Dzubinski's composition. It travels from raw to lyrical and back in the course of just under 4 minutes, with both finesse and energy. - Cliff Furnald, editor
Find Prism Quartet online.
items._genre: contemporary classical / chamber music / spoken word / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: 这张作品由作曲家David Dzubinski创作，Prism Quartet萨克斯四重奏联合诗人Ursula Rucker、打击乐家Tyshawn Sorey及小提琴家Carlos Santiago共同演绎。作为「Unlocking Your Inner Composer」系列合作项目的一部分，作品在不到四分钟内从粗粝的原始张力走向抒情的旋律表达，再回归起点，展现出对动态与情绪层次的精准把控。评论者强调四重奏在跨界合作方面的探索一贯具有打破类型边界的特质，融合器乐、人声与打击乐的编制形成了多层次的对话结构。这首作品既是当代古典语境的延伸，也是与自由即兴、诗歌吟诵及实验声响的交汇，适合关注跨界融合的听众作为入门切入点。

items._cn_summary: 本文为实验音乐聚合乐评，介绍了两张近期作品。Blair Coron 的《Woven Ground》将当代作曲与影像融合，把视觉与音乐作为同一项目的组成部分处理，强调多媒体整体性。Sunken Cages 的《Neram Pularumbol》则将南印度节奏传统带入电子音乐语境，探索文化根源与电子手段之间的对话空间。两张作品均属于跨媒介或跨文化实验范畴，但原文为汇编式短评，信息量有限，无法深入判断其声音设计的独特程度与艺术成就。整体而言内容指向明确的小众实验音乐领域，但因篇幅过短且为转载性质，参考价值受限。

items._cn_summary: 本文为爵士杂志的专辑评论合集，核心介绍的是布莱顿乐团 Hill Collective 的第二张专辑《Fire In Orbit》。乐团扎根于精神爵士传统，强调即兴演奏的松散感与粗糙质感，不回避演奏中暴露的原始边缘，整体比首张作品更为精简与聚焦。同篇还提及 Chris Coull Quartet 携手歌手 Imogen Ryall 的《Fluidian》，但正文内容仅为引言段落，评论正文被截断，缺少对具体音乐结构、编曲细节与演奏语境的深入分析。读者仅能获得风格定位与乐队地理来源等基本信息，无法据此评估实际听感与艺术价值。

items.body: Deathrock has always had a practical relationship with bad news. A macabre sense of mortality supplies the subject matter, punk supplies the impatience, and everyday life keeps renewing the subscription. East Bay four-piece Normal Weirds bring those concerns together on Frown Time, a title that sounds reasonably restrained given the circumstances. Released October 2, the band’s second full-length gathers ten songs that push further into deathpunk and deathrock while retaining their anarcho-punk roots and post-punk unease. The band’s own description, “deathrock gloom dragged through the dirt of punk,” gives a useful indication of the record’s priorities: atmosphere, abrasion, and the urgency of having something unpleasant to get off your chest. Normal Weirds released their debut album, Same Difference, in 2024, followed by the six-song EP No Lease On Life in 2025. The debut examined growing up and working free of the circumstances that had already laid out a person’s future. Taken alongside that earlier record, Frown Time suggests a widening field of concern, with individual frustration meeting the larger sense that the whole arrangement is becoming increasingly fucked. Driving basslines and hard, direct drums provide the foundation, with guitars moving between wiry punk attack and darker passages thickened by effects. Urgent, sometimes theatrical vocals heighten the unease, while lean arrangements preserve the roughness of the band’s approach. The emphasis stays on noise, tension, and the force of the playing, giving their darker direction a distinctly physical edge. The band offers Rudimentary Peni, Cemetery, T.S.O.L., and Chain Cult as points of comparison. “Deathpunk” feels like a useful shorthand for the territory they describe, where punk aggression and deathrock atmosphere share the same cramped quarters. Across their releases, Normal Weirds have increasingly brought those impulses together, giving the darker material a harder and more direct frame. Mortality, alienation, and everyday absurdity run through the album’s lyrical concerns. Its ominous mood draws on both personal experience and a broader disillusionment with the present. There is a bluntness to the title that suits that outlook: Frown Time makes room for the irritation and apprehension people are often expected to swallow while getting on with their day. Frown Time was recorded, mixed, and produced by Skot Brown of Altar De Fey and mastered by Greg Wilkinson. The album is available to stream and purchase on Bandcamp here. It will be released on other streaming platforms, excluding Spotify, on October 16, 2026. Listen to Frown Time below: Frown Time by Normal Weirds Follow Normal Weirds: Instagram Facebook YouTube Bandcamp Linktree The post East Bay Deathpunks Normal Weirds Stare Down Mortality on New Album “Frown Time” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: Normal Weirds的第二张全长专辑收录十首曲目，将死亡摇滚的阴郁氛围与硬核朋克的攻击性进一步融合。贝斯线条沉稳推进，鼓点硬朗直接，吉他则在尖锐朋克冲击与厚重音效暗色段落之间切换。人声紧迫且带有戏剧化色彩，强化了不安的整体基调。歌词围绕死亡、疏离与日常荒诞展开，既来自个人经验，也映射对当下更广泛的失望。专辑由Altar De Fey的Skot Brown录制、混音及制作，Greg Wilkinson负责母带处理。乐队借鉴的参考包括Rudimentary Peni、Cemetery、T.S.O.L.与Chain Cult，延续了从首张专辑到EP以来不断收窄两种冲动之间距离的方向，使阴郁素材获得更硬朗直接的框架。

items.body: Karine Polwart has proved herself to be an exceptional talent as a singer and songwriter for many years, all the way back to her time with Malinky (the song �Thaney� was a revelation). As a solo artist she�s grown and continually expanded her horizons, coming now to Windblown , a project that began life seven years ago, when Polwart, along with sound designer and composer Pippa Murphy, was artist in residence at Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh. The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. Find the artist online. Sara Serpa - Encounters and Collisions (Review) Karine Polwart- Laws of Motion (Review) Live in the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, 2025

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑源于苏格兰皇家植物园的驻留项目，以园中最古老的一棵棕榈树为核心意象，讲述其生长、倒下与种子新生的循环。整张作品以人声与钢琴为主，配合精炼的声音设计与环境采样，营造出内敛而庄严的氛围。Polwart温暖而富有同情心的嗓音与Milligan的钢琴形成默契对话，反复出现的旋律短句如同钩子般留在听者记忆中。虽然表面形式简约，但作品试图从一棵树延伸至历史、自然与人类记忆的宏大叙事，将植物学、植物园的空间感与苏格兰民谣传统结合。专辑、舞台演出与书籍三位一体的呈现方式拓展了音乐项目的外延，让听者从被动欣赏转变为主动参与者。对于偏好实验声响或先锋融合的听众而言，作品本身的实验性较弱，但其概念性与跨界叙述方式仍提供了一定的聆听价值。

items.body: Sudan Dudan is a Norwegian duo, Marit Karlberg and Anders Erik R�ine, who have released four albums over the last twenty years. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. All in all a fine, imaginatively conceived and beautifully produced record, available as a download or vinyl. Find the artists online. items.body:
The musical partnership between Kalaniemi and Alakotila has thrived over a remarkable 35 years, long enough to the Finnish pair to develop a stunning intimacy and telepathy. Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
There�s a sense of calmness to the work here, a long, sweet exhalation between two instrumentalists who are deep enough in sync to allow seamless improvisation beyond any written score and carry the listeners along with them. For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.
Morgondimma
There are several original pieces alongside the tradition, with Kalaniemi�s �Hambo Vid F�bodan� a real standout, and it�s perhaps inevitable on any disc featuring accordion that a Piazzolla tune should be included, brings its own shadows to the whole (�Oblivion�). And, this being Finland, a tango is almost obligatory, in this case Alakotila�s �Tango Berlin.�
Tango Berlin
There�s a gentle, dreamlike quality to so much of this, flowing and mellifluous. The pieces aren�t an arena for showy virtuosity. Instead, the two musicians serve the tune, exploring and genuinely enjoying their performances.
It won�t shake the earth, but it makes for some true listening beauty.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张芬兰手风琴与钢琴二重奏专辑，两位音乐家合作长达三十五年，默契深厚。专辑以传统北欧民间曲调为基底，Kalaniemi的手风琴演奏注重旋律歌唱性，Alakotila的钢琴不仅提供和声支撑，还加入个人发挥，使每首作品都打磨成精致的宝石。整体氛围安静平和，如两人之间悠长的呼气，允许大量超越乐谱的无缝即兴流淌。曲目涵盖多首原创作品与改编的传统曲，包括一首皮亚佐拉的探戈曲和一首芬兰风味的探戈，并偶尔加入弦乐四重奏与无歌词人声。音乐不追求炫技，而是服务于旋律本身的探索与享受，呈现出温柔梦幻、如蜜般流畅的特质。
